Infant mucosa injures easily and bleeds, and the flexible catheter conforms to the small passages with far less trauma. It does not increase pressure, it is not intended for tracheal use at this level, and it depends on the same suction source as any other catheter.

Long-standing lung disease raises pulmonary vascular resistance, and the right ventricle eventually fails against that load, backing fluid into the systemic veins and producing dependent swelling. Coughing does not injure the kidneys, and neither intake volume nor positional venous pooling explains the chronic pattern in this setting.

Raising inspired oxygen concentration increases the amount carried to the cells, which is the point of the therapy. Respiratory rate may change as a consequence but is not the goal, carbon dioxide production is determined by metabolism, and cough strength depends on muscle function and volume rather than oxygen concentration.

Coughing and audible sounds prove air is still moving past the obstruction, and the patient's own cough is more effective than any intervention. Silence, progressive cyanosis with declining consciousness, and inability to speak all indicate that essentially no air is passing.

Stridor and a muffled voice with drooling both localize to structures at or above the larynx, where swelling or a foreign body restricts flow on inspiration. Diffuse expiratory wheezing and a prolonged expiratory phase reflect narrowing of the bronchioles well below the larynx.

A rate of four cannot sustain adequate minute ventilation regardless of the oxygen concentration offered, so positive pressure at a normal rate is the immediate need. A passive mask requires effective spontaneous breathing, and both vital signs and a secondary survey come after life threats are managed.

Excessive positive pressure ventilation keeps intrathoracic pressure elevated, impeding blood return to the heart and lowering output and pressure. Cardiac output falls rather than rises, carbon dioxide is driven down rather than up, and coronary perfusion suffers along with everything else.

The oral adjunct is reserved for patients who cannot protect their own airway, shown by absent gag reflex and obstruction from the tongue. A patient who resists, one who is alert and speaking, and one actively vomiting all retain reflexes that make the device dangerous.

Distended neck veins, hypotension, and muffled tones with clear lungs form the classic triad of fluid restricting ventricular filling. A tension pneumothorax would abolish sounds on one side, pulmonary edema produces crackles, and an asthma exacerbation produces wheezing with a prolonged expiratory phase.

Loss of muscle tone allows the tongue, anchored to the mandible, to fall back against the posterior pharynx, which is why maneuvers that displace the jaw forward relieve the obstruction. The other structures may contribute to airway noise but are not the usual cause of positional obstruction.

Needing to sleep upright describes orthopnea, which develops when redistributed fluid congests the lungs in the supine position. A pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, and aspiration all begin abruptly and do not produce a progressive, position-dependent pattern over days.

The device delivers a high fixed flow that can overdistend and injure immature lung tissue and force air into the stomach, which is why it is generally avoided in pediatric patients. It connects to standard supplies, delivers high concentration, and is designed for apneic patients.

Sliding the tip along the inside of the cheek keeps it away from the sensitive midline structures that trigger gagging and reduces the chance of pushing material deeper. Midline insertion and upward angling both provoke the gag reflex, and the rigid device is not used nasally.

Air accumulating in the stomach raises gastric pressure until contents pass back into the pharynx, where they can be aspirated, and the distended stomach also pushes the diaphragm upward and limits lung expansion. Diaphragmatic rupture is not a consequence, and neither oxygen content nor airway patency improves.

Only the tension variety builds enough pleural pressure to compress the great vessels, producing hypotension with distended neck veins and eventually tracheal shift. Reduced unilateral sounds, pleuritic pain, and tachypnea with anxiety occur with both, so none of those separates the two.

Asking the patient identifies the emergency and obtains consent, and confirming the absence of speech, cough, and air movement establishes that the obstruction is complete. Hand placement above the navel precedes the thrusts themselves, which are repeated until the object clears or the patient loses consciousness.

Minute ventilation is tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate, which is why both depth and rate must be assessed together. Tidal volume is the amount per breath, residual volume is what remains after full exhalation, and vital capacity is the maximum volume that can be voluntarily exchanged.

Children in respiratory arrest with a perfusing rhythm are ventilated at roughly 20 to 30 breaths per minute, matching their higher metabolic demand. Adults, including those in arrest with an advanced airway and those with agonal breathing, are ventilated at about 10 per minute.

Debris and blood must be cleared before anything is inserted or any pressure is applied, or the material is driven into the lungs. Inserting an adjunct first pushes debris deeper, ventilating first aspirates it, and the nasal route is avoided with midface trauma.

The number of words a patient can produce per breath is a practical measure of how much air is available, and two- to three-word phrases indicate severe limitation. Mild exacerbations permit full sentences, and the finding is an objective measure rather than an indication of exaggeration or a laryngeal problem.

Measuring from the nostril to the earlobe approximates the distance from the nares to the posterior pharynx, where the tip should sit. The other measurements produce a device that is either too long, extending past the target and possibly into the esophagus, or one sized for the oral route.

Carbon monoxide from an engine in an enclosed space binds hemoglobin in a way the standard sensor reads as saturated, so the number is unreliable and high-concentration oxygen is continued to displace it. In the other situations the reading reflects actual oxygenation and further oxygen offers no benefit.

Only the bag-valve mask pushes gas into the lungs independent of the patient's own effort, which is what defines positive pressure ventilation. The cannula and the two mask types all depend on the patient generating a spontaneous breath to draw the oxygen in.

An irregular rhythm predisposes to clot formation, and the sudden onset of pleuritic pain with clear lung fields fits obstruction of pulmonary blood flow rather than a problem with the airways or alveoli. Pulmonary edema produces crackles, bronchitis produces a productive cough with wheezes, and hyperventilation does not cause pleuritic pain.

Drowsiness with a slowing rate signals carbon dioxide retention and fatigue, and wheezing that vanishes while effort remains unchanged means too little air is moving to make the sound. Longer sentences and reduced accessory muscle use both reflect genuine improvement in air movement.

Confirming the adjunct actually improved air movement, and watching for a returning gag reflex, is the immediate follow-up because a misplaced device can worsen obstruction. Taping, applying oxygen, and documenting all follow the reassessment that establishes the airway is better than before.

Maintaining both an airtight seal and forward jaw displacement with one hand is the most difficult part of the skill, and leak around the mask is the usual reason volume fails to reach the lungs. Flow rate, bag size, and reservoir capacity affect oxygen concentration rather than whether volume is delivered.

Air in one pleural space prevents that lung from expanding fully, producing decreased or absent sounds on the affected side while the other side remains normal. Bilateral crackles indicate fluid, bilateral wheezing indicates diffuse bronchoconstriction, and bilateral silence with deviation is not the pattern of a simple pneumothorax.

Each positive pressure breath transiently raises pressure inside the chest, and stacking breaths keeps that pressure elevated so blood cannot return to the heart, dropping output and perfusion. Oxygen concentration per breath does not fall, reservoir behavior is a supply issue, and tongue position is unrelated to rate.

A forceful cough generates more airflow than any intervention available, so the priority is to encourage it while watching for signs that exchange is becoming inadequate. Thrusts, sweeps, and repositioning are all reserved for obstruction that becomes complete or for a patient who loses consciousness.

Anaphylaxis can recur hours after initial improvement, so those patients need continued observation regardless of how well they look. Complete resolution after a single bronchodilator dose, a mild cough with normal vitals, and pain reproduced by palpation do not carry the same risk of abrupt deterioration.

An oversized adjunct can push the epiglottis over the laryngeal opening and worsen obstruction, so it is exchanged for the correct size. Partial insertion leaves the tongue unsupported, modifying the device creates sharp edges and unpredictable behavior, and using the wrong size risks the obstruction it is meant to relieve.

Saturation reflects the outcome of the patient's effort, not how much effort it costs, so a normal number in a patient using accessory muscles means compensation is intact but may not last. The clinical picture establishes genuine distress, the device is not necessarily faulty, and oxygen and close monitoring remain appropriate.

Verifying adequate pressure and a properly seated regulator with an intact washer prevents both running out mid-transport and a dangerous high-pressure leak. Temperature is irrelevant, a compressed gas cylinder cannot be checked by shaking, and a hiss at the valve indicates a leak rather than readiness.

A patient who has already vomited and cannot protect the airway is likely to do so again, and having suction ready at the head is the single most useful preparation. A second adjunct adds nothing, withholding oxygen harms the patient, and a head-down position worsens the risk of aspiration.

The bluish discoloration appears when a significant portion of hemoglobin is carrying no oxygen, making it a late and serious sign of inadequate oxygenation. Carbon dioxide levels, blood volume, and temperature all affect the patient in other ways but do not directly produce this color change.

Firm resistance means the passage is blocked or the angle is wrong, and forcing past it causes bleeding that complicates the airway further, so the opposite nostril is tried instead. Watering eyes and mucus on the device are common and harmless, and reaching the flange quickly means insertion succeeded.

A simple mask without a reservoir delivers roughly 40 to 60 percent because room air is entrained through the side ports with each breath. Twenty-four percent corresponds to a low-flow cannula, and concentrations near or above 90 percent require a reservoir system or positive pressure with a tight seal.

Recent surgery or prolonged immobility raises the probability of a clot obstructing pulmonary circulation, which fits sudden dyspnea without infectious features. Sleep side preference, diet, and ambient temperature do not meaningfully change the differential for an abrupt onset at rest.

Swelling below the level of any adjunct cannot be relieved by devices at this level, so maximizing technique with two rescuers while moving quickly toward advanced airway capability is the best available action. Thrusts address a foreign body rather than tissue swelling, a second adjunct adds nothing, and a passive mask cannot ventilate an apneic patient.

Mild hypoxia in an alert patient with adequate effort is best corrected with modest supplemental flow that can be increased if the response is inadequate. Assisted ventilation is for inadequate breathing, a fixed high-flow device exceeds what this patient needs, and withholding oxygen leaves a correctable deficit untreated.

Gurgling in an unresponsive patient means fluid is sitting in the airway with no protective reflexes to clear it, and aspiration occurs within seconds. A strong cough, an audible voice, and an adequate rate all indicate the patient is still moving air and protecting the airway.

Matching bag size to patient size reduces the chance of delivering volumes that overdistend immature lungs and force air into the stomach. Oxygen concentration depends on flow and the reservoir rather than bag size, the connections are standard, and a reservoir is still needed for high concentration.

A sudden onset during eating points directly to material entering the airway, particularly in children and older adults with swallowing difficulty. Fever developing over days suggests infection, exercise onset suggests bronchospasm, and worsening when supine suggests congestion.

At least 10 liters per minute is needed to keep the reservoir filled between breaths, and most protocols specify 12 to 15. Lower flows allow the bag to collapse during inspiration, which means the patient draws room air through the valves and receives far less oxygen than intended.

An adjunct keeps soft tissue off the posterior pharynx, but the head and jaw still have to be positioned so that the airway axis is open. Adjuncts come in pediatric sizes, remain in place during ventilation, and have no effect on oximetry readings.

Extensive pulmonary congestion accompanied by hypotension indicates cardiogenic shock, where the ventricle can no longer generate adequate output, and prognosis is far worse than with congestion alone. Diuretic-induced dehydration would not cause crackles, and neither adequate compensation nor a primary lung cause fits the combination.

A slow rate with shallow depth produces inadequate minute ventilation, and no amount of oxygen offered passively will correct it. A faster rate with good excursion, a mildly reduced saturation with intact speech, and a strong cough all indicate air is being moved adequately.

Orthopnea develops when lying flat redistributes fluid into the pulmonary circulation and is a hallmark of congestive heart failure. Apnea is the absence of breathing, tachypnea is an abnormally fast rate, and hypoxia is inadequate oxygen at the tissue level.

Clearing the secretions and using gravity to keep more from pooling protects a patient who is otherwise breathing adequately. An oral adjunct is not indicated when reflexes are intact, positive pressure is unnecessary with adequate effort, and a mask over an unprotected airway does nothing about the fluid.

Once an advanced airway is secured, compressions are delivered without pause and ventilations are given asynchronously at about 10 per minute. The thirty-to-two ratio applies before an advanced airway, breathing every three seconds hyperventilates the patient, and fifteen to two is a pediatric two-rescuer ratio.

Serious conditions including early embolism and cardiac ischemia can present with breathlessness before objective findings appear, so a normal initial set of numbers does not exclude a significant problem. Dismissing the complaint, assuming a psychological cause, or waiting for deterioration all risk missing a time-sensitive condition.

Gagging means the tip has reached the hypopharynx and is stimulating the gag reflex, so the device should be withdrawn slightly. The flange resting at the nostril indicates correct depth, minor bleeding reflects mucosal irritation, and relief of snoring is the intended outcome.

Assisting requires both a clinical indication, such as wheezing with increased effort, and confirmation that the medication belongs to this patient. A patient with no complaint has no indication, and an unresponsive patient cannot generate the inspiratory effort needed to use the device.

Gas follows the path of least resistance, so a leak means much of each squeeze escapes around the mask rather than entering the lungs, producing poor chest rise. Concentration does not rise, the valve is not affected by leaks, and exhaled gas is directed away from the reservoir by design.

Bronchiolitis follows a viral upper respiratory illness and produces wheezing with copious secretions in the small airways of infants. A barking cough with stridor describes croup, sudden choking suggests a foreign body, and fever with drooling suggests a supraglottic infection.

A sudden fall to near zero most often means exhaled gas is no longer reaching the sensor, which points to tube displacement or a circuit disconnection and requires immediate confirmation. Slowed compressions cause a gradual decline, tank pressure does not affect the reading, and return of circulation causes an abrupt rise rather than a fall.

Suctioning removes oxygen along with secretions, so raising the oxygen reserve beforehand reduces the hypoxia that follows each pass. Bilateral adjuncts serve no purpose, a head-down position is not routine, and blood pressure measurement does not change how the airway is cleared.

Audible escape at the connection means the seal is not seating properly, which wastes oxygen and can create a dangerous high-pressure release. A gauge near 1,800 to 2,000 psi is normal for a full cylinder, frost from gas expansion is expected, and a steady flowmeter ball indicates correct function.

Because the tongue attaches to the mandible, displacing the jaw anteriorly pulls the tongue away from the posterior pharyngeal wall without moving the neck. The trachea is not stretched, compressing the palate would obstruct rather than open, and the maneuver specifically avoids head extension.

Visible vomitus in an unresponsive patient will be aspirated with the next breath, making suction the immediate priority. A patient managing his own secretions, one with dry membranes, and one with a dry cough all have airways that are clear of material requiring removal.

Symptoms that appear reliably with exertion and resolve with rest indicate that the system can meet resting demand but not increased demand, which is the signature of reduced cardiac or pulmonary reserve. Obstruction and allergic reactions do not follow exertion so predictably, and the reproducible pattern argues against a purely psychological cause.

Preoxygenating builds a reserve before oxygen is removed, measuring prevents inserting the catheter past the oropharynx, insertion without suction avoids mucosal trauma and unnecessary oxygen loss, suction is applied on withdrawal, and ventilation with reassessment follows every pass.

Giving the therapy the patient will accept delivers some benefit immediately while continued coaching may gain acceptance of the better device. Forcing a mask on a competent patient is battery, and withholding oxygen because the ideal device was refused punishes the patient for exercising a valid choice.

Early compensation raises rate and effort while mentation remains intact aside from anxiety. A falling rate with drowsiness marks decompensation, cyanosis with agonal breathing marks failure, and absent sounds without movement indicates arrest.

The therapy requires an awake, cooperative patient with spontaneous effort, and it works well by pushing alveolar fluid back and reducing the work of breathing. Unresponsiveness, suspected pneumothorax with hypotension, and active vomiting are all recognized contraindications.

A patient who responds to voice retains protective reflexes, and inserting an oral device is likely to trigger gagging and vomiting. Cardiac arrest, unresponsive overdose without a gag reflex, and apnea during ventilation all describe patients who cannot protect the airway and benefit from the adjunct.

Immune and cough responses weaken with age, so older adults often present with confusion, weakness, or decreased appetite rather than the classic febrile picture. Antihistamines, prior infection, and household composition do not account for the absence of the typical signs.

A collapsing reservoir means the patient's inspiratory demand exceeds the flow being supplied, so the flow is increased until the bag stays at least partly inflated. Switching devices lowers the concentration delivered, reducing flow worsens the problem, and loosening the straps allows more room air to be entrained.

Persistent snoring after correct positioning means soft tissue is still obstructing, and an adjunct maintains what the manual maneuver could not hold alone. Oxygen flow cannot overcome an obstruction, a collar addresses spinal concerns rather than patency, and prone positioning makes both assessment and ventilation impossible.

Anaphylaxis is defined by systemic involvement, most importantly airway compromise or circulatory collapse, rather than by the severity of the skin findings. Localized itching, ocular and nasal symptoms, and an isolated rash all describe reactions that have not become systemic.

Without a sealed airway, a compression delivered while the bag is squeezed raises pressure sharply and drives gas into the esophagus, causing distention and aspiration risk. Concentration, valve integrity, and reservoir refilling are not what the coordination protects against.

The recovery position lets secretions and vomit drain from the mouth rather than pool in the pharynx. A supine patient with a pillow risks aspiration and airway flexion, an upright unresponsive patient cannot maintain the position, and prone placement prevents airway access entirely.

Inadequate ventilation is the immediate threat regardless of how it developed, and assisted breaths correct both the carbon dioxide accumulation and the hypoxia. Removing oxygen from a patient who is now hypoventilating causes hypoxia, and both a low-flow device and watchful waiting leave the ventilation problem untreated.

Chest rise confirms volume is entering the lungs, and an improving saturation confirms that volume is accomplishing gas exchange. Resistance at the bag can mean obstruction, mask condensation only shows some air movement, and silence at the edges does not prove air went to the lungs rather than the stomach.

Fever with purulent sputum and crackles limited to one area indicates consolidation from infection. Embolism typically produces clear lungs with sudden pleuritic pain, a pneumothorax produces decreased sounds without fever, and heart failure produces bilateral basal crackles rather than a focal finding.

Keeping delivered volume to the minimum that produces chest rise keeps airway pressure below the point at which the esophagus opens. Holding breaths in and ventilating rapidly both raise mean pressure, and a larger bag makes it easier to deliver excessive volume rather than harder.

Cyanosis appears only after a substantial amount of hemoglobin is carrying no oxygen and therefore represents advanced hypoxia. Restlessness, an increased respiratory rate, and an increased heart rate are all early compensatory responses that appear well before the color change.

Recording how the patient responded establishes whether the intervention worked and guides the receiving team's next decisions. Equipment brand, which crew member assisted, and restocking time may appear in records for other purposes but contribute nothing to the clinical picture.

Carbon monoxide exposure makes the oximeter reading unreliable, and cardiac arrest involves profound circulatory failure where maximal oxygen delivery is indicated. A minor laceration and a sprained ankle with normal vital signs involve no impairment of oxygenation.

Drowsiness with a falling rate indicates the patient is failing and needs both ventilatory support and rapid transport. A wheeze that cleared, a mild wheeze with intact speech, and wheezing only on forced exhalation all indicate adequate air movement.

Gas taking the esophageal route distends the abdomen while the chest fails to rise, which is the signature of excessive pressure or volume. A climbing saturation shows the technique is working, condensation shows exhaled gas is returning, and reservoir refilling reflects adequate oxygen supply.

A clenched jaw prevents oral insertion but leaves the nasal route available. An absent gag reflex favors the oral device, and both clear nasal drainage and a suspected basilar skull fracture are reasons to avoid the nasal route entirely.

Oximetry reports one variable, the percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen, and says nothing about how hard the patient is working or whether carbon dioxide is being cleared. Ventilation adequacy and carbon dioxide retention require other assessments, so the device supports rather than replaces clinical judgment.

Without a reservoir, each squeeze draws in room air and delivers a far lower concentration, so the reservoir is what allows delivery approaching 100 percent. The pop-off valve limits pressure, the adapter changes the connection, and an exhalation filter affects infection control rather than concentration.

Taking over ventilation manually removes the uncertainty of a malfunctioning device and lets you assess the airway directly. Adjusting settings is outside the scope at this level, a face mask bypasses the functioning route, and waiting delays support for a patient in active distress.

A returning level of consciousness means protective reflexes are returning, and leaving the device in place invites gagging, vomiting, and aspiration. Securing the device, leaving it in with oxygen added, and upsizing it all keep an oral device in a patient who can no longer tolerate one.

Synchronizing assisted breaths with the patient's own efforts augments the volume of each breath without fighting the patient's timing. Random or expiratory-phase delivery opposes the patient's effort and raises airway pressure, and waiting for full apnea allows preventable hypoxia.

Bracing the arms gives the shoulder and chest wall muscles a fixed point to pull against, which improves chest expansion when the diaphragm alone is not enough. It does not lower metabolic demand, redistribute pulmonary blood flow meaningfully, or slow the heart rate.

AVPU grades level of consciousness, and the first letter marks a patient who is awake and aware without needing stimulation. Airway patency, motor function, and pulse quality are assessed separately and are not what this scale measures.

Spurting arterial bleeding is an immediate life threat and is controlled during the primary assessment rather than deferred. A deformed forearm, a medication allergy, and a mildly elevated pressure are all findings that belong to the secondary assessment and history.

Central circulation is assessed at the carotid in an unresponsive adult because peripheral pulses may be absent in shock while central perfusion persists. The radial is used in responsive adults, the femoral is less accessible with clothing in place, and the brachial is the infant site.

Any purposeful or reflexive movement generated only by a painful stimulus places the patient at the P level. Verbal responsiveness requires a reaction to voice alone, alertness requires spontaneous awareness, and the unresponsive level means no reaction to any stimulus.

The final element captures what the patient was doing immediately before symptoms began, which often points directly to the cause. Physical findings, onset timing, and contact information are gathered elsewhere in the assessment and documentation.

Respiratory rate is determined by counting the number of complete breathing cycles in a measured period, usually 30 seconds doubled. Pulse rate is counted at an artery, blood pressure requires a cuff, and skin temperature is assessed by touch.

Patients unconsciously alter their breathing when they know it is being watched, so the count is taken while attention appears to be elsewhere. Announcing the count, instructing the patient to breathe normally, and having the patient count all draw attention to the act of breathing.

Shunting blood away from the skin toward the core, together with sweat gland stimulation, produces the cool, pale, moist combination characteristic of shock. Vasodilation produces warm flushed skin, increased delivery would produce pink warm skin, and lost vascular tone produces warm dry skin below the injury.

A unilaterally enlarged pupil suggests pressure on the oculomotor nerve from rising intracranial pressure or herniation and is a critical finding. Brisk equal reaction, equal size in the normal range, and dilation in low light are all normal responses.

The general impression is a rapid judgment that sets the urgency of everything that follows, made largely from what is seen and heard on approach. Definitive diagnosis is not an EMT function, mechanism documentation occurs in the narrative, and consent is a separate legal step.

Unresponsiveness with inadequate breathing is an immediate threat to life and defines a high-priority patient. An isolated closed fracture, a controlled nosebleed, and chronic ankle pain all involve intact airway, breathing, and circulation.

Compartment intrusion indicates the forces reached the occupants directly and correlates with serious injury. A cracked windshield alone, airbag deployment with minor damage, and scattered glass indicate a collision occurred but not necessarily one that transferred severe energy.

Recognizing early that more hands, a rescue crew, or advanced care is needed is a size-up function because those resources take time to arrive. Hospital wait times, report wording, and driving assignments have no bearing on the immediate safety and resource needs of the scene.

A systolic below 90 with a rapid thready pulse indicates compensation has failed and perfusion is inadequate. The other readings all represent pressures compatible with adequate perfusion, particularly when accompanied by a strong pulse and warm dry skin.

Increasing pressure inside the skull triggers a reflex rise in blood pressure to maintain cerebral perfusion, and the baroreceptor response slows the heart, together with irregular respirations. A falling pressure with a rising pulse is the pattern of hypovolemia, and the other combinations do not reflect this reflex.

The primary assessment moves in sequence from airway to breathing, checking rate, depth, and effort before circulation is evaluated. Peripheral pulse quality comes with circulation, and deformities and history belong to the secondary assessment.

Capillary refill is measured by blanching a nail bed and timing the return of color, normally under two seconds. Sternal pressure is used to test response to pain, lip color is a general perfusion observation, and comparing warmth assesses skin temperature rather than refill.

As the body compensates for volume loss, vasoconstriction raises diastolic pressure while falling stroke volume lowers systolic, squeezing the two together. Improvement would widen the pulse pressure, and the finding combined with tachycardia is too consistent to dismiss as measurement error or a normal resting variant.

Providers come first because an injured rescuer adds a patient and removes a caregiver, followed by the crew, then uninjured bystanders, then the patient. Every alternative ordering places someone ahead of the providers whose ability to help depends on remaining uninjured.

An unresponsive patient cannot report symptoms and the mechanism suggests multiple possible injuries, so a rapid full survey is indicated. An isolated finger laceration, isolated ankle pain, and a chronic rash all permit a focused examination of the area involved.

A rapid weak pulse with pale skin indicates inadequate perfusion, and treatment with rapid transport begins during the primary assessment rather than waiting. A detailed exam, a complete vital sign set, and a medication list all occur en route once the life threat is being addressed.

The P asks what makes the symptom better or worse, which helps distinguish causes such as musculoskeletal pain that changes with movement from cardiac pain that does not. Position, prior episodes, and past history are useful but are gathered elsewhere in the history.

The normal adult range at rest is roughly 60 to 100 beats per minute. Forty-four is bradycardic in most adults, and both of the higher rates represent tachycardia that usually reflects pain, fever, hypoxia, hypovolemia, or a dysrhythmia.

Loss of the radial pulse indicates peripheral perfusion has fallen far enough that the extremity is no longer receiving adequate flow. A regular rate in the normal range, warm dry skin, and brisk capillary refill all indicate perfusion is being maintained.

Involuntary rigidity and guarding suggest peritoneal irritation from blood, infection, or leaked contents, which is a surgical concern. A soft abdomen, mild localized tenderness, and present bowel sounds all suggest a far less acute process.

Prehospital stroke scales assess facial droop, arm drift, and speech abnormality, which together detect the great majority of large vessel strokes. Pupil response, capillary refill, and breath sound comparison are useful assessments but are not part of these scales.

An active disturbance is an unsecured scene, and staging out of sight until law enforcement clears it prevents the crew from becoming part of the violence. Entering, announcing yourself at the door, and waiting in the doorway all place providers within reach of an unpredictable situation.

Life threats can develop at any point, so the airway, breathing, and circulation are rechecked whenever anything changes and at regular intervals during transport. Assessing only once, only at the hospital, or only on request would allow a deterioration to go undetected.

Delayed capillary refill and a weak rapid pulse both reflect reduced flow to the periphery as the body compensates for inadequate circulating volume or pump function. A normal respiratory rate with clear lungs and normally reactive pupils do not indicate a perfusion deficit.

Compensatory mechanisms narrow the vessels and speed the heart, holding pressure near normal until roughly a third of blood volume is lost, which is why pressure is a late indicator. Oxygen demand does not fall on command, blood loss does affect pressure eventually, and a faster pulse does not by itself raise pressure.

Full orientation in all four categories represents the highest level of mental status documentation. It does not specifically test cranial nerves, does not confirm any particular glucose value, and does not exclude a head injury, since a patient can be fully oriented early after significant trauma.

Unstable patients are reassessed at least every five minutes because their condition can change rapidly and the trend guides treatment. Stable patients with minor complaints and normal findings are reassessed at longer intervals, commonly every fifteen minutes.

Inflating past the point where the pulse disappears ensures the artery is occluded, and slow deflation allows the first and last sounds to be heard accurately. A fixed high inflation is uncomfortable and unnecessary, the brachial artery is the correct listening site, and clothing under the cuff distorts the reading.

Reading the placard from upwind at a distance identifies the hazard without entering a potential contamination zone. Walking up to read it defeats the purpose, assuming the trailer is empty ignores the warning, and delaying identification exposes the crew before the risk is known.

No air movement is an immediate threat requiring ventilation without delay. Slow scalp bleeding is controlled with pressure during the secondary phase, prior cardiac history informs the assessment, and nausea alone does not threaten life in the next minutes.

Asking the patient to describe the sensation elicits terms such as crushing, tearing, or burning that help distinguish causes. The other questions explore provocation, time, and radiation, which are separate components of the same history tool.

A rate of six produces inadequate minute ventilation and hypoxia within minutes, so ventilatory support comes first regardless of the suspected cause. Glucose testing, a neurological exam, and positioning all address information or comfort rather than the immediate threat.

Hot flushed skin reflects vasodilation and a raised core temperature, which accompanies infection and heat emergencies. Cool clammy skin suggests shock, cool skin with a bluish tint suggests poor oxygenation or cold exposure, and warm dry skin of normal color is the normal finding.

Scene size-up establishes safety and resource needs before contact, the primary assessment identifies and treats immediate life threats, the secondary assessment and history gather detail, and reassessment tracks whether the patient is improving or deteriorating.

Counting patients is a size-up function because it determines whether the resources on scene are sufficient before care begins. Breathing adequacy, level of consciousness, and pulse presence are all elements of the primary assessment performed at the patient's side.

Vasoconstriction raises diastolic pressure and narrows the pulse pressure while tachycardia maintains output, which is exactly how compensated shock appears before pressure falls. Dismissing the picture as normal, attributing it to anxiety, or assuming pressure must be low all miss a patient who is compensating and can decompensate quickly.

The M gathers prescribed, over-the-counter, and recreational substances the patient uses, which frequently explains the presentation or limits treatment options. Mechanism, mental status, and prior medical visits are documented but are not this element of the mnemonic.

Every second spent searching for a pulse is a second without circulation in a patient who may be in arrest, so the check is limited and compressions begin if no pulse is definitely felt. Accuracy does not worsen with time, and neither occlusion nor rhythm disturbance is the reason for the limit.

Pain that can be reproduced precisely by palpation points to the chest wall rather than the heart, though it never fully excludes a cardiac cause. Associated nausea and diaphoresis, radiation to the arm and jaw, and onset with exertion all raise the suspicion of ischemia.

Understanding the forces involved directs the search for injuries that have not yet produced symptoms, particularly internal ones. Legal responsibility is not an EMS determination, destination decisions rest on protocol and patient condition, and no mechanism replaces a hands-on exam.

Blood in the mouth of a patient with diminished protective reflexes will be aspirated, making suction and positioning immediate priorities. A strong cough, full-sentence speech, and loud crying all demonstrate a patent airway with adequate air movement.

Medical identification jewelry often names conditions such as diabetes, seizure disorder, or anticoagulant use that immediately change the assessment. Vehicle details, bystander count, and ambient temperature rarely provide comparable clinical information, though environment can matter in specific exposures.

Signs are findings the provider can observe or measure, and a counted respiratory rate qualifies. Reported breathlessness, dizziness, and chest tightness are all sensations only the patient can perceive, which makes them symptoms.

An irregular rhythm means beats are not evenly spaced, so a short sample multiplied upward can be substantially wrong and a full minute is counted instead. The shortened counts are acceptable only for regular rhythms, and estimating from a display does not confirm which beats actually produce a pulse.

An unresponsive patient with a mechanism suggesting a fall cannot report pain or neurological symptoms, so the spine is protected until it can be evaluated. A finger laceration, a chronic cough, and nontraumatic abdominal pain provide no mechanism to suggest spinal injury.

Duration since the symptom started belongs to the time element, which also captures whether the symptom has changed since it began. Onset describes what the patient was doing at the start, severity is the intensity rating, and region describes where the pain is located.

A falling level of consciousness and a weakening peripheral pulse both indicate perfusion is deteriorating. A small rise in systolic pressure within the normal range and a rate settling toward normal with good depth both represent improvement or normal variation.

Absent normal breathing in an unresponsive adult requires a rapid pulse check to determine whether compressions are needed. A full survey, a blood pressure, and a medication search all delay the decision that determines whether the patient is in cardiac arrest.

Moving a bariatric patient safely requires more hands and equipment rated for the weight, and calling early prevents both patient and provider injury. There is no hazardous material involved, air transport is a destination decision unrelated to lifting, and no security issue has been described.

The lowest level on the scale describes a patient who does not react to voice or to painful stimulus. History, pupil findings, and vital sign stability are all documented separately and are not what this letter measures.

The mnemonic directs a systematic search for deformities, contusions, abrasions, punctures, burns, tenderness, lacerations, and swelling in each body region. Circulation checks, history elements, and consent issues are all assessed, but not through this particular tool.

The jaw thrust relieves tongue obstruction without moving the cervical spine, which is why it is the trauma maneuver of choice. Head-tilt and turning the patient both move the spine unnecessarily, and delaying airway management for immobilization allows preventable hypoxia.

Each patient is his own control, so differences in strength, sensation, pulse, or movement between sides point to injury even when the patient has not noticed it. Comparison adds time rather than saving it, pulses should be equal bilaterally, and no comparison is required before taking vital signs.

Flexing the hips and keeping still reduces tension on an irritated peritoneum, which is why patients with peritonitis avoid movement. Breathing difficulty leads to an upright position, low cerebral perfusion leads to lying flat, and musculoskeletal pain usually varies with position rather than demanding stillness.

Sensory pathways and motor pathways travel in different parts of the cord, so preserved sensation with lost movement indicates incomplete injury affecting the motor tracts. A complete transection abolishes both, bilateral peripheral nerve injury would not spare sensation so selectively, and the deficit clearly indicates injury.

Agonal gasps do not move meaningful volume and are functionally equivalent to apnea, requiring immediate positive pressure. A rate of 22 with equal rise, wheezing with intact speech, and a productive cough all show the patient is moving air.

Resource requests are driven by how many patients require care and how sick each one is, since each critical patient needs a dedicated crew. Transport distance, bystander numbers, and time of day influence logistics but do not set the number of units needed.

Nausea is a sensation only the patient can perceive and report, which defines a symptom. Pale skin, a counted pulse, and observed pupil size are all findings the provider can see or measure, making them signs.

An undersized cuff requires more pressure to compress the artery, so the measured value exceeds the true pressure. An oversized cuff produces the opposite error, cuff size clearly affects accuracy, and sounds are still audible even when the reading is wrong.

Severe bleeding is a circulatory life threat and is controlled during the primary assessment before moving on. Bowel sounds, temperature, and grip strength are all part of a more detailed examination performed after life threats are managed.

Touching the skin, typically on the forehead or trunk, gives a direct assessment of relative temperature and moisture. The patient's perception can be misleading, color reflects perfusion rather than temperature, and ambient air comparison does not assess the patient at all.

The rapid survey proceeds from the head and neck downward through the chest and abdomen to the pelvis and extremities, which keeps the examination systematic and ensures the regions containing the most immediate life threats are examined first.

Calling for help before committing to patient care ensures units are en route while triage begins, since resources requested later arrive later. Beginning definitive care on one patient, loading everyone into one unit, and performing full assessments all delay the call that brings the needed help.

The primary assessment exists to find and correct problems that will kill the patient in the next minutes, working through airway, breathing, and circulation. Determining causes, collecting history, and documenting are all important but occur after life threats are addressed.
Adults at rest normally breathe between 12 and 20 times per minute. The 20 to 30 range is normal for a toddler, rates of 6 to 10 are bradypneic in an adult, and 30 to 40 is the infant range.

Pain traveling from one location to another describes radiation, which can point to specific causes such as aortic or renal pathology. Provocation addresses what changes the pain, severity is its intensity, and onset is what the patient was doing when it began.

Rigidity and distention with tachycardia suggest blood accumulating in the abdominal cavity, which can be a large and rapid volume loss. A small abrasion, isolated joint pain, and a localized shin bruise all reflect minor superficial injury.

The device reports one variable and is interpreted together with effort, mentation, and lung sounds. It does not replace a respiratory rate count, cannot alone determine oxygen need, and becomes unreliable when peripheral perfusion is poor as in severe hypothermia.

Declining consciousness signals an evolving threat to the airway and perfusion, requiring frequent rechecks of the basics. Stable minor wounds, chronic complaints, and patients declining transport after minor events do not carry the same risk of rapid deterioration.

Provider safety governs at every stage of the call, so the crew moves to safety and brings the patient if that can be done without added risk. Staying in place, sending the patient out alone, and finishing an assessment first all keep providers in a dangerous environment.

Loss of sympathetic tone below a cord injury produces hypotension without the expected tachycardia and leaves the skin warm and dry rather than cool and clammy. Hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock both produce tachycardia with cool moist skin, and anaphylaxis typically includes airway or skin manifestations.

A difference in volume between sides suggests a unilateral process such as pneumothorax, consolidation, or a mainstem obstruction, and careful comparison localizes it. Equal sounds, clear fields with a normal rate, and the absence of adventitious sounds are all normal findings.

The brain tolerates reduced flow poorly, so confusion, agitation, or drowsiness often appear before other measurable changes. Blood pressure changes reflect compensation, pupil changes appear late in intracranial emergencies, and skin temperature reflects peripheral rather than cerebral perfusion.

A rising rate means the patient is working harder to hold the same saturation, which is a compensatory change that can be followed by fatigue and failure. Treating a stable saturation as reassuring, dismissing the trend, or reducing monitoring all miss the significance of increased effort.

Anticoagulation greatly increases the risk of continued bleeding and of delayed intracranial hemorrhage after even a minor head impact. Recent food intake, the ability to walk, and a family history of cholesterol problems do not change the immediate risk from this injury.

Index of suspicion is the expectation of particular injuries formed from the mechanism, which keeps the provider looking for damage that has not yet declared itself. It is not certainty, it does not describe trust in the history, and it is not a measure of scene hazard.

Posture, color, and difficulty producing speech are visible within seconds and together indicate a patient in serious trouble. Sitting up and conversing, standing and gesturing, and walking unassisted all suggest adequate perfusion and airway function.

Allergies and last oral intake are two of the SAMPLE elements, which build a general picture of the patient. What changes the symptom and how intense it is are provocation and severity, both components of the focused pain assessment.

Time on scene is minimized for critical patients, so detailed assessment happens en route to definitive care. A stable minor complaint allows a full assessment on scene, and neither patient seating preference nor family requests should drive the decision about where the exam happens.

The earliest reliable response to volume loss is an increase in heart rate while vasoconstriction keeps pressure near normal. Bradycardia with a normal pressure, tachycardia with hypertension, and bradycardia with hypotension all describe patterns seen in other conditions rather than compensated blood loss.

Safety precedes everything else because providers who become injured cannot help anyone and add to the workload. Patient count, mechanism, and equipment selection all follow the determination that the scene can be entered.

A thready pulse is weak and faint, reflecting a low stroke volume with peripheral vasoconstriction, and is commonly found in shock. Bounding describes an unusually forceful pulse, irregularity describes rhythm, and variation with breathing describes a different phenomenon entirely.

The pediatric assessment triangle uses appearance, breathing effort, and circulation to the skin to form an impression without touching the child. Blood pressure falls late in children, the underlying sequence mirrors the adult approach, and children compensate strongly before deteriorating rapidly.

Sudden confusion with sweating in a patient who takes insulin fits a falling glucose level closely. Gradual onset with weight loss suggests a chronic process, unilateral neurological deficits suggest stroke, and days of fever with cough suggest infection.

Palpation detects the return of the pulse, which marks systolic pressure, but provides no way to identify the diastolic value. Palpated readings tend to run slightly lower rather than higher, position is not a requirement, and the method can be used with an irregular pulse.

Serious injuries, particularly internal ones, can be silent early, so mechanism alone justifies a complete assessment. Releasing the patient, examining only where it hurts, and transporting without evaluating all risk missing an injury that has not yet produced symptoms.

Placing the vehicle between oncoming traffic and the work area creates a physical barrier that protects everyone operating at the scene. Parking beyond the scene removes that barrier, turning off lighting reduces visibility, and working in an active lane exposes the crew directly.

A persistently elevated heart rate means a driving problem such as volume loss, pain, hypoxia, or fever remains, even though mentation improved. Recording recovery, reducing monitoring, and downgrading priority all treat one improved finding as though the whole picture had normalized.

Visible distention with the patient upright indicates backpressure in the venous system, which occurs with right heart failure, tamponade, or tension pneumothorax. Normal hydration does not distend the neck veins when seated, venous oxygen content is not visible, and the finding involves veins rather than arteries.

Producing clear speech requires air to move past the vocal cords, which directly demonstrates a patent airway. Chest symmetry, a saturation reading, and a strong peripheral pulse all provide useful information but none of them confirms that the airway itself is open.

Consistency in the scale used makes changes in the reported number meaningful, which is what allows the trend to guide treatment. Comparisons to past injuries are subjective, facial expression varies widely between people, and a single measurement provides no trend at all.

Several people affected in the same space points to something in the environment, and it is also a warning that the crew is at risk. A seizure history, an old empty bottle, and the time or place a patient was found do not carry the same implication of an ongoing environmental hazard.

Warm pink dry skin with refill under two seconds shows blood is reaching the periphery in adequate volume. Mottling with delayed refill, pallor with a weak pulse, and cyanosis with cool fingertips all indicate that flow to the extremities is compromised.

Mental status is a direct window on cerebral oxygen and blood delivery, making it an early and sensitive indicator of how sick the patient is. Destination decisions, refusal capacity, and family contact all follow from the assessment rather than being its purpose.

Eye opening that requires a spoken stimulus places the patient at the verbal level of the scale. Spontaneous opening would indicate alertness, requiring a painful stimulus would be the next level down, and unresponsiveness means no reaction to any stimulus.

Level of consciousness is established first because it drives every decision that follows, then the airway is opened and evaluated, then breathing is assessed for rate and adequacy, and finally circulation is checked with control of any major bleeding.

Autonomic symptoms such as nausea with sweating and onset during exertion both point toward ischemia, where increased demand outstrips supply. Pain reproduced by palpation and pain that varies with arm position both point toward the chest wall rather than the heart.

A segment of ribs broken in multiple places moves opposite to the rest of the chest wall, drawing inward as the rest expands. Symmetrical expansion, a superficial bruise, and equal breath sounds do not indicate a free-floating segment of chest wall.

Height determines the energy delivered on impact, and falls exceeding roughly three times the patient's height are considered significant. Falling on carpet from standing, breaking a fall with a hand, and having witnesses present do not describe high-energy mechanisms.

Visual scales and gestures allow a patient to communicate severity without shared language, and interpreters should be used when available. Vital signs are influenced by many factors, silence does not indicate mild pain across cultures, and omitting the assessment leaves treatable pain untreated.

Turning the patient as a unit with manual head stabilization allows airway and breathing assessment while limiting spinal movement. Assessing adequately in the prone position is not possible, dragging by the arms twists the spine, and waiting delays assessment of possible life threats.

A tearing quality with radiation to the back is a classic description for aortic dissection, a time-critical vascular emergency. A strain does not typically produce this quality, gastrointestinal causes rarely present this way, and the description does not exclude cardiac disease.

Absent pulse means circulation has stopped, and compressions are started without delay to move blood to the brain and heart. A blood pressure cannot be measured without circulation, adjunct placement follows compressions, and a trauma survey is irrelevant until circulation is being supported.

Whether doses have been taken, missed, or doubled frequently explains the presentation and guides treatment decisions. Cost, pharmacy name, and container color contribute nothing clinically, though the label itself may help identify the drug.

The short neck of an infant makes the carotid difficult to locate reliably, so the brachial artery in the upper arm is used. The radial pulse is often too faint to assess in infants, and the temporal artery is not a standard pulse assessment site.

Hypertension with bradycardia and an irregular respiratory pattern form the triad indicating dangerously elevated pressure within the skull. Hypovolemia produces tachycardia with falling pressure, pain raises rather than lowers heart rate, and neurogenic shock produces hypotension rather than hypertension.

When the patient cannot provide history, family, bystanders, medication bottles, and the scene itself become the sources. Recording that none was available, assuming a psychiatric cause, and withholding treatment all fail a patient whose inability to communicate may itself be a sign of serious illness.

A grain bin is a confined space with engulfment and atmospheric hazards, and entry requires specialized training and equipment that EMS crews do not carry. Entering with a partner, entering alone, or assessing from inside all place untrained providers in an environment that regularly kills would-be rescuers.

A heart rate returning toward normal alongside improving color indicates perfusion is recovering and compensatory demand is falling. A rising heart rate, a falling pressure, and increasing respiratory effort all suggest the patient is deteriorating rather than improving.

Instability indicates a fracture, and repeated manipulation can disrupt clots and worsen bleeding into the pelvic space. Reported tenderness without instability, a superficial abrasion, and normal alignment do not carry the same risk from continued examination.

The triangle uses appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to the skin to judge severity before contact, which avoids agitating the child prematurely. It supplements rather than replaces hands-on assessment, does not yield a diagnosis, and has nothing to do with transport logistics.

Recording specifically what was declined along with the explanation given protects both the patient's care and the provider, and tells the receiving team what remains unknown. Documenting only what was done, labeling the patient uncooperative, and assuming normal findings all leave the record misleading.

Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic values, and 20 is well below the normal range of roughly 30 to 40, consistent with vasoconstriction and a falling stroke volume. The values given are sufficient to calculate it, and a narrow difference is neither widened nor normal.

Air transport is justified when time to definitive care meaningfully changes outcome for a critical patient. Patient preference, minor injuries at accessible locations, and crew convenience do not justify the added expense and risk of a helicopter response.

Severe external hemorrhage is a life threat and is controlled the moment it is identified, without waiting for the rest of the assessment. Obtaining vitals, moving to the ambulance, and finishing a secondary survey all allow continued blood loss that can be stopped in seconds.

Family members know the patient's normal behavior, and their report of a change is often the most reliable evidence available. Slow answers, anxiety about transport, and repeated questions may simply reflect personality, stress, or hearing difficulty rather than a change from baseline.

Mental status and pulse both change as perfusion changes, making them the most informative repeat measurements in an unstable patient. Allergy history and mechanism are fixed facts established once and do not require repeated assessment.

Standard measurement places the cuff over the brachial artery on the upper arm with the lower edge above the antecubital fossa. Forearm and wrist placement produce inaccurate readings with standard equipment, and thigh placement is reserved for situations where the arms cannot be used.

Rapid extrication trades spinal precautions for speed and is justified only when an immediate life threat cannot be corrected where the patient sits. Stable neck pain, an isolated wrist injury, and patient anxiety all permit a controlled removal with full precautions.

Low blood glucose is a rapidly reversible cause of confusion with sympathetic findings, and measuring it directly answers the most likely question. Cardiac tracing, abdominal palpation, and pupil measurement all provide information that will not change the immediate treatment as directly.

Aging alone does not cause disorientation, so new or worsening confusion is investigated as a sign of illness such as infection, hypoxia, or medication effect. Assuming age-related confusion, treating a known baseline as a reason to stop assessing, and dismissing the importance of changes all risk missing serious illness.

Multiple people in the same dwelling with headache and nausea during heating season is the classic pattern, and the gas itself is odorless. A single febrile patient, an isolated rash, and an outdoor odor all point elsewhere, and the absence of a smell does not exclude the gas.

Adequate breathing requires both a rate in the normal range and sufficient depth, demonstrated by equal bilateral expansion. A fast rate with minimal movement, irregular gasping, and rapid shallow breathing with accessory muscle use all describe inadequate ventilation requiring support.

The L records when the patient last ate or drank, which matters for surgical planning and for interpreting diabetic emergencies. Complaint location, level of consciousness, and symptom duration are all documented but come from other parts of the assessment.

A facial droop points to stroke and starts a time-sensitive pathway that changes destination, notification, and urgency. Poor sleep, a remote history of similar symptoms, and a hospital preference may all be documented but do not change the immediate clinical approach.

Having the patient perform simple movements and press against resistance tests both movement and strength without moving the spine. Lifting limbs passively moves the patient unnecessarily, painful stimuli are reserved for unresponsive patients, and self-report alone does not test function.

A visible restraint mark indicates substantial force transmitted to the abdomen, and internal injuries can bleed silently while compensation keeps vital signs normal. Releasing the patient, limiting assessment, and delaying decisions all rely on findings that appear normal precisely because compensation has not yet failed.

Standard precautions assume that any patient's blood and body fluids may transmit infection, which protects against the many carriers who are unaware of their status. Reserving protection for known infections, visible blood, or reported history all leave gaps where exposure is most likely to occur unnoticed.

Crackling under the skin indicates air escaping from the airway or lungs into the tissues, which signals a significant injury to those structures. A superficial scratch, jewelry, and a tattoo are all incidental findings with no bearing on the urgency of care.

A change in condition means the life-threat picture may have changed, so the airway, breathing, and circulation are rechecked and treatment adjusted accordingly. Continuing unchanged, deferring to the hospital, and simply driving faster all leave a potentially correctable problem unaddressed.

With reduced circulating volume, standing shifts blood to the lower body, producing a rise in heart rate and a fall in pressure. The other patterns do not describe the compensatory response to position change in a volume-depleted patient.

A pulsating mass suggests an aortic aneurysm and rigidity with tachycardia suggests peritoneal irritation with developing shock, both time-critical. Improvement after vomiting and mild localized tenderness both describe presentations that are far less likely to deteriorate rapidly.

Recording both gives the receiving team the full picture, while treatment follows what is actually observed, since findings do not depend on recall or willingness to disclose. Recording only one side loses information, and asking the patient to resolve the discrepancy assumes he can.

Hypotension with altered mentation indicates that perfusion is failing, which defines an unstable patient. A normal pressure with mild pain, normal lungs with a normal pulse, and an isolated extremity injury all describe patients whose perfusion is intact.

Weapons are handled by law enforcement, and withdrawing until the scene is secured protects the crew and preserves evidence. Moving the weapon yourself, involving the patient in handling it, and taking it into the ambulance all create safety and legal problems.

Responsiveness establishes immediately whether the patient can protect the airway and communicate, and it directs the entire assessment that follows. Insurance, recent meals, and living situation may all appear later in the record but tell you nothing about immediate stability.

The pattern cycles from shallow to deep and back, punctuated by pauses, and is associated with brainstem injury or severe systemic illness. Consistently deep rapid breathing describes a different pattern associated with acidosis, and both irregular gasping and fixed shallow breathing describe other abnormal patterns.

When life threats are present and cannot be fully corrected on scene, a brief assessment precedes rapid transport with further evaluation en route. A sprained wrist, a chronic cough, and mild abdominal discomfort all allow a complete assessment before moving.

A pertinent negative is the documented absence of a symptom you specifically asked about because it would be expected with the suspected condition. A recorded pulse is a measurement, and both reported pressure and observed diaphoresis are positive findings rather than negatives.

Comparing circulation before and after shows whether the splint has compromised blood flow, which requires immediate adjustment. Pulse checks at a limb do not measure systemic pressure, do not confirm fractures, and do not assess pain tolerance.

Known violent behavior changes how and whether the crew enters, and may require law enforcement first. Hospital preference, recent meals, and housekeeping may all be documented later but do not bear on whether entry is safe.

Tripod positioning combined with short phrase speech indicates the patient is working hard to move air and has limited reserve. Treating the patient as stable, assuming a psychiatric cause, or dismissing the presentation all ignore objective evidence of severe distress.

Bilateral pinpoint pupils with sluggish reaction are characteristic of opioid effect, particularly with depressed respirations. Orbital trauma affects one side, bright light produces brisk equal constriction that recovers, and an expanding mass typically causes a unilateral dilated pupil.

Pathology such as consolidation, a pneumothorax, or focal fluid may be audible in only one area, so limited listening can miss it entirely. Full auscultation takes longer rather than shorter, is not how rate is counted, and does not validate an oximetry reading.

Blood rapidly saturating a dressing indicates ongoing uncontrolled hemorrhage that must be addressed immediately. A small amount of blood on a bandage, a developing bruise, and dried blood from an old injury all indicate bleeding that is either minor or already stopped.

The coronary arteries branch from the aorta just above the valve and perfuse the myocardium, which is why their blockage causes a heart attack. The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs, and the carotid and brachial arteries supply the head and the arm.

Angina reflects a temporary supply and demand mismatch and resolves when demand falls, while infarction involves ongoing tissue death that rest does not relieve. Pressure quality, hypertension history, and central location are common to both and do not separate them.

Nitroglycerin dilates vessels and can drop blood pressure sharply, so a systolic value above the protocol threshold must be confirmed first. Respiratory rate, glucose, and pupils are all part of the broader assessment but none carries the same direct risk with this medication.

Both drugs dilate blood vessels through related pathways, and giving them together can cause a profound and dangerous drop in blood pressure. Aspirin absorption and oxygen effectiveness are unaffected, and the medication history does not make the pain any less likely to be cardiac.

Women more often present with atypical features such as unusual fatigue, nausea, and discomfort in the back or jaw rather than classic chest pressure. The classic radiating pattern occurs in both sexes, and reproducible or positional pain points away from ischemia.

Adult compressions are delivered to a depth of about two to two and a half inches, deep enough to generate flow without excessive injury. An inch is too shallow to move blood, three inches risks significant injury, and pulse palpation during compressions is unreliable as a depth guide.

A rate between 100 and 120 balances adequate blood flow against the need for the heart to refill between compressions. Slower rates generate insufficient output, and faster rates shorten filling time so much that each compression moves less blood.

A no-shock advisory means the rhythm is not one defibrillation can correct, and compressions are the only intervention that maintains perfusion, so they resume at once. Repeating analysis, prolonging the pulse check, and removing the pads all interrupt the circulation the patient depends on.

A documented allergy is an absolute contraindication because a reaction can be severe. Advanced age, prior nitroglycerin use, and a cholesterol history are not reasons to withhold aspirin from a patient with suspected cardiac chest pain.

Focal deficits affecting one side point to a localized interruption of cerebral blood flow, while low glucose typically produces global confusion. Sweating with cool skin favors hypoglycemia, and both conditions can begin abruptly in patients with chronic medication use.

The time the patient was last seen at baseline determines eligibility for time-sensitive treatments at the receiving hospital. Sleep, handedness, and recent meals do not change the destination decision or the urgency of transport.

A conscious patient who can protect his airway and swallow can be given oral glucose, which raises the blood sugar directly. Withholding treatment prolongs a reversible emergency, water provides no glucose, and insulin would lower the level further.

The body compensates for metabolic acidosis by breathing deeply and rapidly, and ketones produce the characteristic breath odor. Cool clammy skin, sudden onset, and rapid improvement with glucose all describe hypoglycemia instead.

Protecting the patient from injury while the seizure runs its course is the only intervention needed during the active phase. Restraint can cause fractures, objects placed in the mouth break teeth and obstruct the airway, and lifting a seizing patient risks injury to everyone.

After the convulsion ends, the brain requires time to recover, producing confusion, drowsiness, and sometimes agitation. An aura precedes the seizure, and the tonic and clonic phases describe the stiffening and jerking that occur during it.

Continuous seizure activity impairs ventilation and dramatically increases metabolic demand, which can injure the brain and requires urgent intervention. It does not establish a chronic diagnosis, it increases rather than removes the need for evaluation, and it does not identify the cause.

Systemic involvement of the airway and circulation alongside skin findings defines anaphylaxis and requires immediate treatment. A localized reaction at the sting site, isolated eye and nasal symptoms, and a delayed rash all describe reactions that have not become systemic.

The outer thigh has a large muscle mass with good blood flow and can be reached through clothing, giving rapid absorption. The upper arm, abdomen, and buttock are not the intended sites for these devices and offer slower or less reliable absorption.

Epinephrine acts quickly but has a short duration, and the underlying allergic cascade can continue after the drug is metabolized, causing symptoms to return. A second exposure is unlikely in transport, the improvement was real, and the medication treats rather than worsens the reaction.

Opioids suppress the respiratory drive and constrict the pupils, producing the characteristic combination of pinpoint pupils with hypoventilation. Dilated pupils with agitation suggest stimulants, hot dry flushed skin suggests anticholinergic effects, and salivation with twitching suggests organophosphate exposure.

Death from opioid overdose results from respiratory depression, so supporting breathing addresses the mechanism that kills. Identifying the substance, gathering history, and searching the scene all provide information but none of them keeps the patient alive in the next few minutes.

Bringing a corrosive back up exposes the esophagus and airway to a second injury, and dilution can cause a heat-releasing reaction or vomiting. Oxygen, an upright position, and prompt transport are all appropriate parts of managing this patient.

Absorption describes a toxin crossing the skin or mucous membranes, which is why decontamination and provider protection are central to management. Ingestion involves swallowing, inhalation involves breathing the substance in, and injection involves a break in the skin delivering it directly.

When the left ventricle fails, blood backs up into the pulmonary circulation and fluid enters the alveoli, producing crackles. Ankle swelling, neck vein distention, and liver congestion all reflect backup into the systemic circulation from right-sided failure.

Even a successful shock leaves the heart with little immediate output, so compressions resume at once to maintain perfusion while the rhythm organizes. A prolonged pulse check, immediate reanalysis, and pausing for breaths all interrupt circulation at the moment it matters most.

The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it generates the pressure needed to perfuse the entire body. The right ventricle pumps to the lungs, and both atria receive returning blood and deliver it to the ventricles below them.

Pressure built up during compressions dissipates within seconds of stopping, and it takes many compressions to rebuild it, so every pause costs perfusion. Analysis timing, chest wall mechanics, and rescuer fatigue are real considerations but not the reason for the limit.

A transient ischemic attack produces stroke-like deficits that clear as flow is restored, but it signals a high risk of a completed stroke soon afterward. Progressive worsening, bilateral permanent weakness, and slow memory decline all describe different processes.

Bright red blood indicates active bleeding from the esophagus or stomach, which can be rapid and life threatening in patients with liver disease. Dehydration, allergy, and muscular strain are all lesser concerns compared with ongoing hemorrhage.

A sudden, maximal-intensity headache raises concern for a subarachnoid hemorrhage and requires immediate evaluation. A gradual tension-type headache, a recurring pattern that responds to treatment, and sinus symptoms all describe far less dangerous presentations.

Contaminated patients spread the substance to providers and vehicles, so decontamination precedes hands-on care. Standard gloves do not protect against most chemicals, moving the patient into an enclosed space concentrates the hazard, and an alcohol wipe does not decontaminate.

Acetaminophen toxicity is characteristically silent early while the liver injury develops over the following days, making appearance a poor guide. Treating the patient as unaffected, supporting a refusal, or using the absence of vomiting as reassurance all risk a preventable death.

Many of these devices produce continuous rather than pulsatile flow, so the absence of a palpable pulse does not mean the patient is in arrest. Compression decisions follow device-specific guidance, other assessment findings remain useful, and rhythm irregularity is not a defining feature.

Placing pads at a distance from the generator avoids shunting energy through the device and damaging it while still delivering current across the heart. Placing pads over the device wastes energy, back-only placement does not create a path through the heart, and withholding defibrillation removes the only definitive treatment.

Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness from a temporary drop in cerebral perfusion, with recovery occurring on its own within moments. Prolonged unresponsiveness, sustained convulsions, and slow decline all describe other conditions entirely.

Fainting without a positional or emotional trigger, particularly while at rest, raises concern for a cardiac cause such as a dysrhythmia. Standing quickly, a rapid full recovery, and a warning of warmth and lightheadedness all fit a benign vasovagal pattern.

Stimulants drive sympathetic activity, producing dilated pupils, agitation, and elevated heart rate and pressure. Slow shallow breathing with drowsiness and constricted pupils with bradycardia both describe depressant or opioid effects.

An adequate systolic pressure protects against a dangerous drop, and confirming the prescription belongs to this patient ensures the right drug and dose. Being medication-naive is not a requirement, and a slow pulse is not a criterion for assisting with this drug.

Confirming arrest establishes that the device is indicated, pads are applied to a bare chest so the device can analyze, the shock is delivered only after everyone is clear, and compressions resume immediately afterward to maintain perfusion.

Blood loss into the gastrointestinal tract is hidden, so perfusion indicators reveal the severity that the visible bleeding may understate. Episode counts, hospital preference, and dietary history do not tell you how much volume has been lost.

Fever with confusion and hypotension suggests sepsis, where infection has progressed to circulatory failure. A mild sore throat, a fever after exertion, and a one-day productive cough all describe illness without evidence of systemic compromise.

Systemic infection produces fever, tachycardia, and vasodilation along with global confusion, rather than the focal deficits of a brain lesion. A facial droop, a thunderclap headache, and one-sided weakness all point to a localized intracranial process.

Identity, quantity, and timing determine which treatments are possible and how quickly they must be given. The patient's explanation, the caller's identity, and routine medication habits provide context but do not drive antidote or decontamination decisions.

Allowing the patient to sit in a comfortable semi-upright position reduces the work of breathing and anxiety without compromising perfusion. Supine with legs raised is used for hypotension, the lateral position offers no advantage here, and walking increases cardiac demand.

Activity raises heart rate and contractility, increasing myocardial oxygen demand at a time when supply is already limited, which can extend the area of damage. Exertion does not reliably lower pressure, block absorption, or change how the pain is interpreted.

As glucose falls, the body releases adrenaline, producing tremor, sweating, and hunger before confusion develops. Deep breathing with a fruity odor, excessive thirst with frequent urination, and gradual weight loss all reflect high rather than low blood sugar.
