A supine position allows the gravid uterus to compress the inferior vena cava, reducing venous return and blood pressure. The tilt is not about fetal positioning, nausea control, or membrane integrity.

The placenta delivers spontaneously and is transported for examination, since missing fragments indicate a risk of ongoing bleeding. Cord traction can cause inversion or hemorrhage, discarding it loses clinical information, and transport is not delayed waiting for it.

A limb presentation cannot deliver vaginally in the field and requires surgical delivery, so rapid transport with positioning to reduce cord compression is the priority. Manipulating the limb, applying traction, and waiting on scene all risk fetal death and maternal injury.

Infants maintain a higher baseline rate because their stroke volume is small and output depends heavily on rate. The adult range is too slow for an infant, rates in the forties indicate severe bradycardia, and sustained rates above 180 suggest a dysrhythmia or severe distress.

A slowing heart rate in a child who is working hard to breathe signals hypoxia severe enough to depress cardiac function, which precedes arrest. Flaring, a rate at the upper limit of normal, and mild retractions all indicate increased effort without that degree of compromise.

Efficient compensatory mechanisms maintain pressure until a large volume deficit exists, after which decompensation is abrupt. Children have smaller absolute blood volumes, cuff readings are not systematically high with correct sizing, and blood loss is not inherently slower.

Pediatric compression depth is proportional, about one third of the anterior-posterior chest diameter, which accounts for widely varying body sizes. A fixed inch is too shallow for most children, adult depth is excessive for small chests, and pulse palpation during compressions is unreliable.

Keeping the child with a caregiver and moving from least to most distressing preserves cooperation for the parts of the exam that matter most. Separation, starting with painful areas, and isolating the child supine all escalate distress and make the assessment less reliable.

Pediatric arrest usually results from progressive respiratory failure and hypoxia rather than a primary cardiac event, which is why airway management is emphasized. Primary dysrhythmias, coronary occlusion, and valve abnormalities are far less common causes in children.

Persistent lethargy after fever reduction is a red flag suggesting the child is genuinely ill rather than simply febrile. A responsive fever, upper respiratory symptoms, and irritability that settles with comfort all fit common viral illness.

Febrile seizures are brief generalized events in young children, typically associated with a rapidly rising temperature. Prolonged focal events, seizures from direct brain infection, and seizures in older children all fall outside this description and warrant investigation for other causes.

A proportionally large tongue occupies more of the small oropharynx and obstructs easily when muscle tone is lost. Pediatric tracheas are narrower rather than wider, the epiglottis is larger and floppier, and the nasal passages are smaller and more easily blocked.

As the brain atrophies with age, the bridging veins stretch across a wider space and tear with relatively minor force. Skull thickness decreases rather than increases with age, blood pressure is not the mechanism, and brain volume decreases rather than expands.

Older adults frequently present with weakness, confusion, or shortness of breath instead of chest pain, which delays recognition. Classic radiating pain occurs but is less reliable, reproducible pain suggests the chest wall, and exertional-only pain describes stable angina.

Beta blockers blunt the heart's response to sympathetic stimulation, so a bleeding patient may maintain a deceptively normal rate. Diuretics affect volume, antibiotics treat infection, and antihistamines do not prevent the compensatory heart rate rise.

An explanation that does not fit the pattern or severity of injury is the classic warning sign and requires reporting. A single shin bruise, a cluttered but adequately supplied home, and an engaged caregiver are not by themselves indicators of abuse.

Facing the patient allows lip reading and facial cues, and clear speech at a normal volume is more intelligible than shouting, which distorts sound. Speaking from behind removes visual cues, routing everything through family bypasses the patient, and writing everything is unnecessary when speech works.

Hypotension and a significantly depressed mental status both indicate that compensation has failed in a child. A heart rate at the top of the normal range and a capillary refill of two seconds are both consistent with adequate perfusion.

A visible presenting part and an uncontrollable urge to push both indicate the second stage of labor with delivery imminent. Two hours of contractions and membranes that ruptured earlier indicate labor is underway without establishing that delivery is about to occur.

A prolapsed cord is compressed by the presenting part, cutting off fetal oxygen, so a gloved hand relieves the pressure during rapid transport for surgical delivery. Replacing the cord, cutting it, and encouraging pushing all worsen fetal compromise.

Newborns lose heat rapidly through a large surface area and wet skin, and hypothermia worsens every other physiological problem. Weight, a full vital sign set, and delivery time are all recorded but none carries the same immediate consequence.

Fundal massage stimulates uterine contraction, which clamps the vessels at the placental site and is the primary field treatment for postpartum hemorrhage. Vaginal packing is not performed, upright positioning does not reduce bleeding, and delaying transport wastes time.
The infant's short neck makes carotid palpation unreliable, so the brachial artery is used. The radial and pedal pulses are frequently impalpable in infants even when perfusion is adequate.

The two-thumb encircling technique produces better depth and consistency when two rescuers are present. Two fingers are used by a single rescuer, and the adult single-hand and two-hand techniques deliver excessive force to an infant chest.

A higher metabolic rate and greater surface area relative to mass mean children cycle through fluid faster, so losses deplete reserves quickly. They have smaller rather than larger reserves, lose fluid through skin and breathing as well, and absorb oral fluids normally.

Simple language, a calm tone, and the presence of a familiar person reduce fear in a patient who cannot process complex information. Detailed explanations overwhelm, restraint escalates agitation, and rushing without explanation increases confusion and resistance.

Multiple prescribers and multiple drugs increase the chance of interactions and duplications that no one is tracking. Long-term use of a single stable medication, a daily vitamin, and maintaining a medication list all reduce rather than increase the risk.

Reduced pain perception combined with a tendency to attribute symptoms to aging leads many older patients to underreport. Pain nerves remain present, painful conditions are more rather than less common with age, and medications do not abolish sensation entirely.

Children require more frequent ventilation than adults because of their higher metabolic rate and oxygen consumption. Ten per minute is the adult rate, six to eight is inadequate for a child, and forty to fifty would cause harmful hyperventilation.

A semi-reclined position with flexed knees provides access to the birth canal and allows control of the delivery. Standing risks dropping the infant, a firm chair blocks access, and a prone position makes delivery impossible.

Drying removes the wet surface driving heat loss and stimulates breathing, the airway is positioned and cleared as needed, breathing and heart rate are then assessed to determine whether further intervention is required, and warmth with ongoing monitoring follows.

Announcing yourself and narrating each step gives the patient the information sight would normally provide. Touching without warning is startling, directing conversation to family bypasses the patient, and volume has nothing to do with vision.

A sunken fontanelle combined with reduced urine output reflects meaningful fluid loss. Crying without tears can be normal in young infants, handling raises the heart rate transiently, and fussiness relieved by feeding suggests hunger.

An unexplained delay between injury and seeking care is a recognized warning sign that warrants careful documentation and reporting. Scraped knees, parental anxiety, and forehead bruises in walking toddlers are all common and expected findings.

A newborn heart rate below 100 usually reflects inadequate ventilation, and positive pressure breaths correct it in most cases. Compressions are added only below 60, continued drying alone allows deterioration, and transport without intervention neglects the treatable cause.

Abruption involves premature separation of the placenta, producing pain and a rigid tender uterus, often with concealed bleeding. Painless bleeding with a soft uterus is characteristic of previa, and neither postcoital bleeding nor a cesarean history distinguishes the two.

Pregnancy does not prevent blood loss, the fetus does not absorb lost blood, and blood pressure typically falls slightly rather than rising.

Appearance assesses how the child's brain is functioning through muscle tone, engagement, ability to be consoled, eye contact, and the quality of speech or cry. Skin findings belong to the circulation component, effort findings to work of breathing, and vital signs are measured separately.

Deceleration forces can shear the placenta from the uterine wall without any visible external injury, threatening both mother and fetus. The fetus is not immune to trauma, abdominal injury risk is not reduced, and abruption bleeding is often concealed.

Pediatric pads or an energy attenuator deliver an appropriate dose for a small child, and adult pads are used only if pediatric equipment is unavailable. Withholding defibrillation entirely removes the only treatment for a shockable rhythm, and back-only placement does not create a path through the heart.

A lodged button battery generates current that burns through tissue within a few hours, making it a true emergency. These batteries do not reliably pass harmlessly, chewing is not required for injury, and the risk applies to children of any age.

Supplying writing materials lets the patient answer fully in his own words. Restricting to yes or no questions loses detail, bypassing the patient disregards him, and assuming impaired mentation from a speech barrier is a serious error.

A hands-off impression is formed first, the child is kept calm with the caregiver because agitation worsens distress, oxygen is offered in a tolerable way, and hands-on assessment with vital signs follows once the child is settled.

A child's head represents a larger fraction of total body mass and typically strikes first in a fall. The skull is thinner rather than thicker, neck musculature is weaker rather than stronger, and the brain moves more rather than less within the skull.

Knowing what the patient could do before the illness reveals how much has changed, which is what indicates acuity. Assuming full independence, relying on the current exam alone, and comparing to others of the same age all miss the individual's own baseline.

A cuff bladder covering roughly two thirds of the upper arm produces an accurate reading in a child. Adult cuffs read falsely low on small arms, the smallest cuff reads falsely high on larger children, and size clearly affects accuracy.

A functioning hearing aid is the simplest way to restore communication with the patient. Removing it isolates the patient, shouting over the absence of the device distorts speech, and defaulting to writing is unnecessary when the device works.

Aging blunts the febrile response, so a serious infection may present with hypothermia or no temperature change at all. Medications do not universally suppress fever, serious infections are more common with age, and thermometers remain accurate.

Prenatal records identify complications such as multiple gestation, placental position, and gestational diabetes, all of which change how the delivery is managed. Financial matters, physician contact, and predictions about cooperation are not the clinical purpose.

Thin fragile skin tears under shear and pressure, so sliding is minimized and contact points are padded. Rapid movement increases shear, gripping forearms tears skin, and adhesive tape removes skin when it comes off.

Poison control provides substance-specific guidance, and the container identifies the product and concentration for the hospital. Inducing vomiting risks a second exposure of the esophagus, dilution can cause harm with some products, and waiting allows injury to progress.

Adolescents often disclose important information only when they have privacy and are addressed as the patient rather than through a parent. Routing questions through parents, presuming dishonesty, and assessing in front of peers all suppress honest reporting.

Ability varies widely, so addressing the patient and matching the pace to his responses respects his actual capacity. Bypassing the patient, presuming incapacity, and applying a one-size-fits-all simplification all fail to meet him where he is.

Knowing the patient's normal condition and what changed distinguishes an acute problem from a chronic one. Staffing levels, inspection records, and activity schedules do not help interpret the patient's current presentation.

Care plans and experienced caregivers provide details about a child's baseline and usual responses that no protocol contains, and they are integrated with standard care. Ignoring the plan discards that information, following it against protocol exceeds authority, and caregivers do not replace the crew.

A forceful cough moves more air than any intervention and indicates a partial obstruction that the child may clear himself. Thrusts, back slaps, and finger sweeps are all reserved for a complete obstruction and may convert a partial obstruction into a complete one.

Significant hypertension and neurological symptoms such as headache with visual change are both hallmarks of preeclampsia. Mild dependent ankle swelling and urinary frequency are both common and expected in late pregnancy.

Withdrawal from interaction and bradycardia in a child still working to breathe both indicate that compensation is failing. Improving color and a stronger cry both indicate better oxygenation and reserve.

A capacitated adult may refuse, but the isolation increases risk, so a clear discussion of risks with family or medical direction involvement and careful documentation is appropriate. Accepting without discussion, transporting against his wishes, and offering minimal advice all fail him in different ways.

Airway and breathing support address the threat that kills first, while history gathering continues in parallel. Oral medication is unsafe in an unresponsive child, inducing vomiting risks aspiration, and waiting for recovery abandons a deteriorating patient.

Both mother and newborn are patients requiring assessment, warmth, and evaluation at the hospital. Separating them, leaving the infant behind, and delaying transport for feeding all leave a newborn without proper evaluation.

Newborns breathe rapidly because of their high metabolic rate and small tidal volume. The adult range is far too slow for a newborn, rates in the single digits indicate severe depression, and sustained rates above 70 indicate significant distress.

Hormonal changes swell the airway tissues while a relaxed esophageal sphincter and delayed gastric emptying raise the aspiration risk. The airway becomes more rather than less difficult, the gag reflex remains, and oxygen demand rises during pregnancy.

A service animal is a working aid the patient depends on, and it accompanies him when transport can be accomplished safely. Leaving it behind, involving animal control, and requiring separate arrangements all separate the patient from a necessary aid.

Rapport and caregiver involvement, with the least distressing steps first, usually gain enough cooperation to complete the assessment. Restraint traumatizes the child, skipping the exam misses injuries, and forcing through protest damages trust and yields unreliable findings.

Bleeding with pain in pregnancy can reflect significant blood loss and threatens both patients, so shock assessment and transport are appropriate. Waiting at home, performing an internal exam, and self-transport all delay or complicate necessary care.

A pacemaker can fail to capture or sense properly, leaving the rate too slow to maintain perfusion, which produces dizziness. The device does not guarantee adequate output, dizziness is not an expected effect, and dysrhythmias can still occur.

Assisting with the patient's own prescribed bronchodilator when indicated relieves bronchospasm quickly, and the response guides further care. Withholding treatment delays relief, giving doses without reassessment ignores the response, and the decision rests on protocol rather than caregiver preference.

A sick child who does not engage or make eye contact is showing an abnormal appearance, which reflects inadequate brain perfusion or oxygenation. Shyness, comfort, and cooperation would not suppress engagement to that degree in a child who is otherwise unwell.

Preparation and positioning come before the delivery itself, the head is supported and the cord checked as it emerges, the shoulders are guided one at a time to control the delivery, and immediate newborn care follows once the infant is out.

Multiple medications can produce symptoms that resemble disease or suppress the signs that would otherwise reveal it. Medications are not always the cause, lists are often accurate and useful, and drugs do not prevent vital signs from being measured.

Structural damage to a child seat is often invisible, so a seat involved in a significant collision is not reused. Visual inspection cannot rule out damage, and neither limited use nor functioning straps establishes that the seat will still protect the child.

Discolored fluid indicates meconium passage, which can be aspirated and requires readiness to support the newborn's airway and breathing. It is not a normal finding, transport is not delayed waiting for a change, and labor cannot be slowed on request.

Caregivers detect subtle changes long before vital signs shift, and their concern is one of the more reliable indicators of serious pediatric illness. Reassurance based on numbers, release at home, and assuming overreaction all discard that signal.

Blunted pain perception combined with chronic background pain means an acute fracture may not stand out. Spinal fractures do cause pain, bone loss does not remove nerve endings, and pain is often present immediately even when it is underreported.

Blow-by delivered by a familiar caregiver provides supplemental oxygen without the struggle that increases demand. Forcing a mask raises oxygen consumption and distress, withholding oxygen leaves hypoxia untreated, and taping a cannula to a resisting child is both ineffective and distressing.

A large clot suggests the uterus may not be contracting adequately, so the fundus is checked and massaged while watching for signs of shock. Blanket reassurance, discontinuing monitoring, and waiting all miss developing postpartum hemorrhage.

Reduced heat production and blunted temperature sensation make older patients vulnerable to hypothermia during transport. Cooling the compartment, removing coverings, and relying on the patient to report cold all allow preventable heat loss.

A length-based tape correlates size with weight and equipment dimensions far more reliably than age, which varies widely in body size. Age estimates, visual comparison, and defaulting to the smallest equipment all produce mismatched sizing.

A heart rate persistently below 60 despite adequate ventilation calls for compressions coordinated with breaths. Continuing ventilation alone ignores the failing circulation, stopping ventilation removes the treatment for the underlying hypoxia, and defibrillation has no role in this situation.

A familiar adult reduces fear, which makes the child more cooperative and the findings more reliable. Responsibility for assessment remains with the crew, older children should answer for themselves where able, and this is not a documentation requirement.

A seizure in late pregnancy suggests eclampsia, and protection from injury with left lateral positioning and rapid transport addresses both mother and fetus. Attempting delivery during convulsions, restraining limbs, and placing objects in the mouth are all harmful.

Objective documentation and reporting through the established process allows the concern to reach agencies that can act on it. Directing the patient to move exceeds the provider's role, ignoring the observation abandons a vulnerable patient, and discussing it with neighbors breaches confidentiality.

Immobilization reduces pain and prevents further injury, and circulation checks before and after ensure the splint has not compromised blood flow. Forced straightening, having the child move the limb, and delaying immobilization all increase pain and the risk of further damage.

Direct contact with a cold surface draws heat away rapidly from a newborn who has little capacity to generate it. Crying, infection risk, and heart rate assessment are not the primary reasons for avoiding cold surfaces.

Gradual position changes allow the cardiovascular system time to compensate, which prevents syncope. Rapid movement and walking both risk a fall, and complete avoidance of position change is impractical during transport.

A rate of 60 or below with poor perfusion in a child is treated as inadequate circulation, and compressions with ventilation are started. Observation, oxygen alone, and waiting for a lower threshold all allow a deteriorating child to progress to arrest.

Tissue is saved for examination at the hospital, transport is not delayed, and emotional support is part of the care. Discarding tissue loses clinical information, waiting for bleeding to stop risks significant blood loss, and ignoring the emotional dimension fails the patient.

Children have relatively fixed stroke volumes, so cardiac output rises and falls largely with heart rate, which is why bradycardia is so dangerous. Output is not independent of rate, does not rise when the rate falls, and is not determined by blood pressure alone.

Professional interpretation produces accurate information and avoids placing a child in the position of relaying sensitive medical details. Using a child translator, raising volume, and limiting to observation all degrade the quality of the assessment.

Repeated vomiting after a head injury suggests rising intracranial pressure, and airway protection with monitoring and prompt transport addresses both risks. Oral fluids worsen vomiting, supine positioning risks aspiration, and delaying transport allows deterioration.

A field delivery cannot be sterile, but using clean materials and maintaining as clean a field as possible reduces infection risk for both patients. Abandoning cleanliness, attempting to delay an imminent delivery, and involving untrained bystanders all add avoidable risk.

Recording both accounts preserves information while a capacity assessment determines how much weight the patient's own account carries. Automatically favoring either side discards information, and removing family may eliminate a useful source of history.

A pink crying newborn with good tone needs only warmth, drying, and observation. Ventilation, deep suctioning, and compressions are all interventions for newborns who fail to establish adequate breathing or circulation.

Hospice patients have documented goals of care that guide which interventions are appropriate, and comfort measures always remain appropriate. Full resuscitation contradicts those goals, withholding comfort abandons the patient, and family cannot override valid documentation.

Rhythmic pain synchronized with uterine tightening points to labor or placental separation rather than the bowel. Relief with defecation, pain with several days of diarrhea, and localized right lower pain with fever all suggest gastrointestinal causes.

Blood leaving an artery is oxygenated and under pressure from the heart, producing bright color and pulsatile flow. Venous blood is darker and flows steadily, capillary bleeding oozes, and internal bleeding is not visible at all.

Direct pressure controls the majority of external bleeding and requires no equipment. A tourniquet is used when direct pressure fails or bleeding is immediately life threatening, and elevation and pressure points are no longer emphasized as primary measures.

A correctly applied tourniquet occludes arterial flow, which stops the bleeding and eliminates the distal pulse. Continued bleeding with a present pulse indicates insufficient tightness, and warmth, color improvement, and comfort all suggest flow is still occurring.

Negative pressure in the large neck veins can draw air into the circulation, producing an air embolism, which is why occlusive dressings are used. Arm sensation, lower extremity swelling, and immediate infection are not the acute concerns with this injury.

The earliest response to volume loss is sympathetic activation, producing tachycardia with restlessness or anxiety. Bradycardia with drowsiness, warm flushed skin, and a widening pulse pressure all point away from compensated hypovolemia.

Moist sterile coverage prevents the exposed tissue from drying while the occlusive layer retains moisture and warmth. Replacing organs risks contamination and injury, dry tight dressings damage the tissue, and leaving them exposed allows rapid drying.

Bruising over the mastoid, along with periorbital bruising and clear drainage from the nose or ears, indicates a fracture at the skull base. A scalp laceration, a positional headache, and forehead tenderness do not localize to the base of the skull.

A lucid interval followed by deterioration is the classic pattern of an expanding hematoma, most often epidural, and is a surgical emergency. Concussion recovery improves rather than declines, and neither a psychological reaction nor an unrelated cause explains this specific sequence.

An occlusive dressing prevents air from entering the pleural space, and monitoring detects a tension pneumothorax that may follow. A porous dry dressing does not seal, packing the wound drives material into the chest, and leaving it open allows continued air entry.

The object may be tamponading damaged vessels, so it is stabilized and left in place for surgical removal. Removing it can cause uncontrollable hemorrhage, pushing it deeper worsens injury, and cutting it flush is only considered when the length prevents transport.

Immobilization prevents sharp bone ends from damaging surrounding tissue and reduces the pain of movement. Realignment is generally limited to restoring circulation, hospital evaluation is still required, and splinting does not by itself control bleeding.

Checking circulation, movement, and feeling beyond the injury detects compromise caused by the injury or by the splint itself. Blood pressure, lung sounds, and pupil assessment are part of the broader evaluation but do not assess the splinted limb.

These findings indicate the splint is compromising circulation, and loosening it may restore flow before permanent damage occurs. Tightening worsens the problem, elevation does not relieve external compression, and ice does nothing for an occluded artery.

Partial thickness injury extends into the dermis, producing blisters, moisture, and significant pain because nerve endings remain intact. Redness alone is superficial, painless white leathery tissue is full thickness, and charring into muscle is deeper still.

Stopping the burning process limits the depth of injury, and a dry sterile covering protects the tissue while limiting heat loss. Ice causes further tissue damage, home remedies trap heat and introduce contamination, and breaking blisters opens the wound to infection.

Circumferential chest burns form an inelastic layer that restricts chest expansion and can compromise ventilation. A small back burn, a superficial forearm burn, and a palm blister are all significant but do not threaten breathing.

Falls exceeding roughly three times body height indicate the energy transfer associated with serious injury, which is a recognized trauma center criterion. Minor lacerations, collisions with minimal damage, and mild soreness do not meet those thresholds.

The concept emphasizes that early definitive care, particularly surgical control of bleeding, improves outcomes for severely injured patients. It is not a rigid sixty-minute rule, does not describe recovery time, and is not an assessment time limit.

Penetrating chest trauma with hypotension requires surgical intervention that only the hospital provides, so scene time is minimized. Isolated fractures, small lacerations, and minor sprains all allow complete assessment before transport.

Compensation maintains pressure and perfusion until reserves are exhausted, after which the decline is rapid rather than gradual. Injuries do not follow a fixed timetable, stable vital signs do not exclude injury, and deterioration does not require a new event.

Hemostatic dressings are packed directly into wounds in areas such as the groin, axilla, or neck where a tourniquet cannot be placed. They require contact with the bleeding source, so surface application and loose wrapping are ineffective, and they are not reserved solely for tourniquet failure.

Abdominal rigidity combined with poor perfusion indicates blood accumulating within the abdominal cavity. Superficial abrasions, a forearm bruise, and a small scalp laceration are all external injuries with limited blood loss.

Paradoxical motion occurs when a segment of ribs is broken in multiple places and no longer moves with the chest wall. Symmetrical expansion, pain with coughing, and sternal bruising can all occur with rib injury but none indicates a free-floating segment.

Unilateral absent sounds with hypotension and distended neck veins with severe distress both reflect rising pleural pressure compressing the lung and great vessels. Chest wall bruising and pain with inspiration occur with many chest injuries and do not indicate tension.

Hypotension and declining mental status both indicate that compensation has failed and vital organ perfusion is inadequate. A mildly elevated heart rate with anxiety and a normal capillary refill are consistent with compensated shock or normal physiology.

Each entire arm represents 9 percent of the adult body surface, with the anterior and posterior surfaces contributing 4.5 percent each. Eighteen percent corresponds to a leg or the anterior trunk, and 27 percent does not correspond to a standard region.

A traction splint counteracts the powerful thigh muscles that shorten the limb and drive bone ends into tissue, reducing pain and bleeding. A lower leg board does not address the femur, a sling and swathe is for upper extremities, and a pillow provides no traction.

Traction applied with a pelvic fracture can worsen displacement and bleeding, making it a contraindication. A closed midshaft fracture with an intact pulse, deformity with pain, and limb shortening are all indications for the device rather than reasons to avoid it.

Stabilizing the object prevents further damage, and covering both eyes limits the sympathetic movement that would otherwise move the injured eye. Removal, pressure, and blinking all risk driving the object deeper or extruding intraocular contents.

Clear or blood-tinged drainage suggests cerebrospinal fluid escaping through a fracture at the skull base, which indicates significant injury and an infection risk. It is not a benign finding, not normal after head impact, and not evidence of a preexisting infection.

Moving the head, torso, and pelvis together as a single unit prevents the twisting and bending that can injure the cord. Dragging by the shoulders, self-movement, and leading with the head all allow independent spinal motion.

Selective protocols clear patients who are alert, have no midline tenderness, no neurological deficit, and no distracting injury or intoxication. Midline tenderness, neurological symptoms, and an unreliable assessment all require precautions to be maintained.

Adding dressings over the original preserves the clot that has begun to form at the wound surface. Removing the dressing disrupts that clot, reducing pressure allows bleeding to continue, and a tourniquet is reserved for bleeding that pressure cannot control.

Lying flat maximizes perfusion to the brain, and leg elevation can improve venous return. Upright positioning reduces cerebral perfusion, lateral positioning offers no hemodynamic advantage, and standing risks syncope.

Some dry chemicals react with water to generate heat, so the powder is brushed away before irrigation begins. Immediate flushing can worsen the injury, neutralizing agents generate heat, and covering without decontamination leaves the chemical in contact with the skin.

Moist wrapping in a sealed container kept cool preserves tissue without freezing it, which maximizes the chance of reattachment. Direct ice contact causes freezing injury, submersion causes tissue damage, and leaving it dry causes desiccation.

The injured brain has lost its ability to autoregulate, so a fall in systemic pressure directly reduces cerebral perfusion and worsens the injury. Skull fractures are mechanical, hypotension has many causes besides cord injury, and pupil inequality reflects pressure on the nerve rather than low blood pressure.

The wound is exposed so the actual source can be found, direct pressure is applied first because it controls most bleeding, a tourniquet follows if pressure fails, and shock treatment with prompt transport continues once bleeding is controlled.

Leaning forward prevents blood from draining into the throat, and pinching the soft part of the nose applies pressure to the usual bleeding site. Tilting back causes swallowing of blood, packing is not performed at this level, and lying flat increases posterior drainage.

Burned tissue loses its elasticity, so swelling beneath it raises pressure until blood flow to the limb is compromised. Circumferential burns are not necessarily full thickness, and neither healing time nor pain level is the acute concern.

Blood accumulating in the abdomen distends it while the heart rate rises to compensate for the volume loss. A soft abdomen with bradycardia, localized tenderness with warm dry skin, and a widening pulse pressure all point away from significant intra-abdominal hemorrhage.

Air transport is justified when it meaningfully shortens the time to definitive surgical care for a critically injured patient. Patient preference, landing convenience, and crew availability are not clinical justifications for the added cost and risk.

A concussion is a functional disturbance without structural bleeding, typically producing confusion, headache, or brief loss of consciousness. Blood collections are hematomas, skull base fractures are bony injuries, and permanent tissue damage describes a more severe injury.

Falling saturation with shallow breathing indicates the patient is splinting so effectively that ventilation is inadequate, which risks hypoxia and pneumonia. Pain with breathing, local tenderness, and bruising are all expected findings with rib fractures.

If air accumulates under pressure in the pleural space, briefly lifting the dressing allows it to escape and can relieve a developing tension. Cleaning, bleeding checks, and pain reduction are not reasons to break the seal on a sucking chest wound.

Each entire leg represents 18 percent of the adult body surface, so both legs total 36 percent. Eighteen percent covers one leg, 9 percent covers one arm, and 45 percent does not correspond to this combination.

Burns involving the face and hands carry functional and airway implications that require specialized care. Small superficial burns, sunburn, and a single fingertip blister can generally be managed without a burn center.

Selective vasoconstriction redirects limited blood volume toward the brain, heart, and lungs at the expense of the skin and abdominal organs. The heart speeds rather than slows, vessels constrict rather than dilate, and oxygen demand does not fall on command.

A second tourniquet placed proximal to the first increases the compressed area and usually achieves occlusion when a single device cannot. Loosening, removing, and periodic release all allow renewed bleeding from an injury that has already defeated one tourniquet.

Rich vascular supply and the large retroperitoneal space mean a pelvic fracture can bleed several liters without any external sign. The bones are highly vascular, bleeding is typically internal rather than visible, and the pelvis does not tamponade its own hemorrhage.

A binder reduces the pelvic volume and helps tamponade bleeding while minimal movement avoids disrupting formed clots. Repeated palpation, multiple log rolls, and bilateral traction all increase movement at the fracture and worsen bleeding.

An airway that cannot be managed in place justifies rapid extrication with manual stabilization, accepting some spinal risk for a greater immediate benefit. Full packaging and waiting for a controlled extrication both delay airway management, and self-extrication is unsafe with a potential spinal injury.

Continuous irrigation directed away from the unaffected eye dilutes and removes the chemical, and it continues throughout transport. Covering without irrigation, brief irrigation with pressure, and keeping the eye closed all leave the chemical in contact with the tissue.

Current travels through the body, damaging tissue along its path and disturbing cardiac rhythm, so both wounds are located and the heart is monitored. Treating only the surface, assuming superficial injury, and applying ice all miss the internal damage that defines electrical injury.

Prolonged compression causes muscle breakdown, and releasing it washes potassium and metabolic byproducts into the circulation, which can cause dysrhythmias and kidney injury. Fractures do not result from release, external bleeding is not inevitable, and pain alone does not explain the physiological collapse.

Application time determines the ischemia duration, which the hospital needs to know, and the effect documents whether bleeding was controlled. Device brand, attempt counts, and patient comfort opinions do not affect subsequent care.

Repeated vomiting with worsening confusion suggests rising intracranial pressure from bleeding or swelling. An improving headache, a controlled scalp laceration, and transient dizziness are all consistent with a minor injury.

Penetrating torso injury and post-injury hypotension are both physiological and anatomical criteria for trauma center care. An isolated finger fracture and a knee abrasion involve minimal energy transfer and no physiological compromise.

A lost distal pulse and increasing pain with pallor both indicate that blood flow beyond the splint has been compromised. Mild swelling and tenderness at the injury site are expected findings with any fracture.

Shock is a failure of perfusion at the cellular level, which is why it can exist with a normal blood pressure. A blood pressure number alone does not define it, the psychological use of the word is unrelated, and internal bleeding and non-hemorrhagic causes produce shock as well.

The liver occupies the right upper quadrant and bleeds substantially when injured, producing pain there with developing shock. Left lower pain with constipation, flank pain radiating to the groin, and sternal burning all suggest other processes.

Shutting down and locking out the power source prevents the machine from restarting and injuring both patient and rescuers. Working near a running machine, having a bystander operate controls, and improvised cutting all create serious danger.

Brief cooling with running water stops the burning process without causing further tissue injury or hypothermia. Direct ice, chemical cold packs, and prolonged immersion all risk deepening the injury and lowering body temperature.

Increased effort and the uninjured lung can maintain saturation until the patient tires or the injury progresses, after which the decline is rapid. Chest injuries do affect saturation, readings are not universally inaccurate, and an injured lung does not expand to compensate.

With reduced circulating volume, each remaining red cell must carry as much oxygen as possible, which supports tissues receiving less flow. Oxygen does not replace volume, does not restore blood pressure, and has no effect on bleeding.

When circulation is intact, splinting in the position found avoids the additional injury that manipulation can cause. Straightening and traction are reserved for compromised circulation, and leaving the limb unsupported allows painful and damaging movement.

Walking does not exclude a spinal injury, so the decision rests on assessment criteria such as midline tenderness, neurological findings, and reliability. Assuming no injury, applying precautions reflexively, and having the patient continue walking all bypass the assessment that should drive the decision.

Replacing the flap in its anatomical position preserves the tissue's blood supply and improves the chance it survives. Removing the flap discards viable tissue, folding it back exposes the wound bed, and a tourniquet is reserved for uncontrolled bleeding.

The energy required to eject an occupant is enough to produce injuries throughout the body, and impact with the ground adds more. Landing surfaces vary, avoiding interior contact does not offset the greater forces, and being thrown clear is associated with far worse outcomes.

Junctional wounds at the groin cannot be controlled with a tourniquet, so wound packing with direct pressure is the appropriate technique. A thigh tourniquet cannot reach above the injury, elevation with a loose dressing does not control arterial bleeding, and distal pressure does not affect flow into the wound.

Burns in enclosed spaces carry a high risk of airway swelling from heat and irritants, which can obstruct rapidly. Surface area estimation matters for fluid planning, and fire cause and property damage are not clinical priorities.

The diaphragm rises well above the costal margin during exhalation, so wounds below the nipple line can enter both cavities. Such wounds are not limited to the chest wall, they frequently involve the diaphragm, and penetrating injuries often bleed internally rather than externally.

Manual stabilization is established before anything else moves the patient, a neurological baseline is documented before movement changes it, the patient is moved as a unit onto the device, and securing with reassessment completes the sequence.

Internal bleeding is stopped only in the operating room, so the destination and the speed of transport both matter. The nearest facility may lack surgical capability, the bleeding cannot be controlled in the field, and a routine pace wastes time the patient does not have.

Immobilization with cold application limits swelling and pain while circulation checks confirm the limb remains perfused. Weight bearing worsens the injury, heat increases swelling early, and manipulation risks further damage to injured ligaments.

Driving carbon dioxide down constricts cerebral vessels, which reduces blood flow to tissue that is already injured. Hyperventilation lowers rather than raises carbon dioxide, has no effect on fracture patterns, and clearly does affect cerebral perfusion.

Fetal survival depends on maternal perfusion and oxygenation, so stabilizing the mother is the most effective fetal intervention available. Assessing the fetus first, assuming reduced maternal risk, and prioritizing fetal monitoring all divert attention from the intervention that helps both.

Venous blood has given up its oxygen, making it darker, and it flows under lower steady pressure. Spurting bright red blood is arterial, oozing is capillary, and distention without visible blood indicates internal bleeding.

Large burns destroy the skin's ability to retain heat, so dry coverage protects the wounds while preventing hypothermia. Wet sheets cause rapid heat loss, ointments interfere with hospital assessment, and leaving burns uncovered increases contamination and heat loss.

Combativeness after head injury frequently reflects hypoxia or increasing intracranial pressure rather than a behavioral problem, and both are treatable. Assuming intoxication, withdrawing, and abandoning the assessment all miss a physiological cause that is worsening.

Vasoconstriction and tachycardia hold pressure near normal until roughly a third of blood volume is gone, so pressure falls late. Measurement remains feasible, pressure does not rise with ongoing loss, and it is ultimately very much related to volume.

Shallow water diving injuries frequently involve the cervical spine, so in-line stabilization is maintained throughout the extraction. Having the patient swim, pulling by the arms, and delaying extraction for a full in-water assessment all risk worsening a cord injury or drowning.

Direct communication between the outside environment and bone makes deep infection a major risk, which is why these injuries need prompt surgical care. Blood loss varies, surgery is usually required, and healing is slower rather than faster.

Unequal expansion with diminished sounds suggests air or blood in the pleural space preventing the lung from expanding. Isolated rib tenderness, a bruise with equal expansion, and shoulder-related pain all suggest less serious chest wall injury.

The wound losing the most blood is addressed first because that is the one threatening life. Working in the order found, starting with minor wounds, and deferring control until a full survey is finished all allow the worst bleeding to continue.

Spinal protection and life threats take priority, and extremity splinting follows once those are managed. Splinting first delays higher priorities, ignoring the injury allows further damage, and asking the patient to hold his own limb is neither reliable nor safe.

Sympathetic control is lost below the injury, so vessels cannot constrict to conserve heat and the patient takes on the environmental temperature. Metabolic rate does not rise, pain perception is unrelated to heat loss, and skin thickness does not change.

The cheek is the one location where an impaled object may be removed, because it can obstruct the airway and bleeding can be controlled from both sides. Stabilizing it in place leaves the airway obstructed, pushing it through worsens the injury, and cutting it does not relieve the obstruction.

Oral intake risks aspiration and can complicate surgery that a shock patient is likely to need, so nothing is given by mouth. Sips, unrestricted intake, and ice chips all introduce material into a stomach that may need to be empty.

Separating the digits prevents them from fusing during healing, and jewelry is removed before swelling makes it a tourniquet. Wrapping fingers together, leaving rings on, and applying compression all cause preventable complications.

Wet clothing accelerates heat loss dramatically, and hypothermia impairs clotting in a trauma patient. Leaving wet clothing on, applying direct heat to the extremities, and delaying all care allow the patient's temperature to continue falling.

Progressive distention indicates ongoing internal bleeding that only surgery can stop, so shock management and rapid transport are the priorities. Abdominal pressure does not control internal bleeding, prone positioning is unhelpful, and waiting for vital signs to change wastes the compensated period.

These checks reveal whether the nerves and vessels beyond the injury are intact, before and after any intervention. They do not diagnose fractures, measure pain tolerance, or establish the mechanism of injury.

The crackling sensation under the skin indicates air leaking from an injured airway or lung, which signals a significant injury. Bruising, fluid accumulation, and allergic swelling all produce different findings on palpation.

Anticoagulation allows intracranial bleeding to continue unchecked, so deterioration can occur hours after an apparently minor impact. A small laceration, an improving headache, and intact memory all suggest a low-risk injury.

A femur fracture can bleed a liter or more into the thigh without any external evidence, which is enough to cause shock. Splint allergy, pain-induced dehydration, and a neurological response do not produce the volume loss that explains shock in this setting.

Turning the patient and the immobilization device together lets the vomit drain while spinal alignment is maintained. Sitting upright is impossible when immobilized, removing precautions risks cord injury, and turning only the head moves the cervical spine.

Full thickness burns destroy the nerve endings along with all skin layers, which is why the burned area itself may be painless. Redness without blisters is superficial, blistering with severe pain is partial thickness, and delayed peeling follows superficial injury.

A tourniquet must be tight enough to stop arterial flow, and the application time is recorded for the hospital. Partial tightening allows continued arterial bleeding into the limb, joint placement prevents effective compression, and covering it hides a device the trauma team must see.

Guarding is muscular tensing in response to palpation and suggests underlying irritation of the peritoneum. Relaxation is a normal finding, abdominal movement with breathing is normal, and a visible pulsation suggests an aneurysm.

Healthy young patients compensate vigorously, holding pressure and mentation normal until they decompensate abruptly. Young people do sustain serious injuries, vital signs remain meaningful, and bleeding rate is determined by the injury rather than by age.

Penetrating abdominal injury requires surgical control of bleeding, so wounds are covered, shock is treated, and the patient moves quickly. Probing worsens the injury, detailed on-scene examination wastes time, and a tourniquet cannot be applied to the torso.

A capacitated patient may refuse an intervention, and the provider's role is to ensure the decision is informed while continuing other care. Splinting against refusal is battery, conditioning transport on compliance is coercive, and withdrawing care abandons the patient.

A visible impact pattern marks where significant energy was transferred, and the organs beneath may be injured even when the patient feels well. External bruising says nothing about the depth of injury and never excludes damage beneath it.

Stopping the bleeding addresses the cause and warmth preserves clotting function while rapid transport reaches definitive care. Oral fluids risk aspiration and cannot replace intravascular volume, and waiting for vital signs to improve wastes the compensated period.

A dilating unreactive pupil suggests pressure on the oculomotor nerve, and rising pressure with a slowing pulse reflects the reflex response to rising intracranial pressure. An improving headache and stable vital signs both suggest the patient is not deteriorating.

Absent distal circulation justifies one attempt at gentle realignment, since restoring flow prevents tissue death. Splinting as found leaves the limb without perfusion, a tourniquet stops what little flow exists, and transporting unsplinted allows further injury.

Helmet removal with two providers maintaining in-line stabilization allows airway access and assessment while limiting spinal movement. Leaving it in place blocks assessment, self-removal produces uncontrolled motion, and cutting the helmet is neither practical nor safer.

Direct pressure controls bleeding from a digit, and the amputated part is preserved separately for possible reattachment. A proximal tourniquet is excessive for a finger, and attempting to reattach or replace the part in the field damages the tissue.

A binder reduces pelvic volume to help control bleeding, and minimal movement preserves any clot that has formed. Repeated rolling, bilateral traction, and waiting for pressure to improve all worsen bleeding or waste time.

Lightning most often kills through cardiac and respiratory arrest, and patients frequently recover with prompt resuscitation. Patients carry no residual charge, surface burns are often minor compared with the internal effects, and spontaneous recovery cannot be assumed.

Lightning arrest patients often respond to prompt resuscitation and rarely have other lethal injuries, so they receive priority in contrast to usual triage. Treating minor injuries first, using discovery order, and prioritizing ambulatory patients all misapply triage principles here.

Warm dry skin with bradycardia after a spinal injury indicates neurogenic shock from lost sympathetic tone rather than hypovolemia. Cool clammy skin, delayed refill, and a narrowing pulse pressure are all consistent with blood loss.

Preventing hypoxia and hypotension while monitoring for changes protects the injured brain more than any other field intervention. Routine hyperventilation reduces cerebral blood flow, extreme head elevation compromises perfusion, and restricting oxygen worsens the injury.

Large burns lose heat rapidly, so dry sterile coverage with temperature monitoring balances wound protection against hypothermia. Extensive wet dressings cause heat loss, breaking blisters opens the wound, and ointments interfere with hospital evaluation.

Assessment proceeds while interpretation is arranged, since time-critical injuries cannot wait for perfect communication. Delaying assessment, relying only on gestures, and assuming no useful history all reduce the quality and timeliness of care.

Leaving the object in place avoids converting a tamponaded wound into an actively bleeding one, and pressure is applied around rather than over it. Removal risks hemorrhage, pushing it deeper causes further damage, and direct pressure drives it further in.

Damaged capillaries leak plasma into the tissues across the burned area, so the larger the area the greater the intravascular loss. Burns do not primarily cause external blood loss, and area does not determine analgesic dosing or healing speed in this calculation.

Sitting upright lets the diaphragm work more efficiently and reduces the pain of chest wall movement. Position does not prevent fractures, does not stop bleeding into the pleural space, and does not remove the need for oxygen.

Airway management with spinal precautions comes first because obstruction kills fastest, breathing is then assessed and supported, catastrophic external bleeding is controlled as part of circulation, and packaging with rapid transport follows once immediate threats are managed.

Pain is expected with a correctly applied tourniquet and is not a reason to loosen or remove a device that is preventing fatal bleeding. Loosening, removing, and repositioning distally all risk renewed hemorrhage.

Sterile coverage protects the exposed bone from further contamination before immobilization. Pushing bone back introduces contamination internally, field irrigation of an open fracture is not performed, and leaving it exposed increases infection risk.

Tingling suggests cord or nerve root involvement, which is documented as a baseline and managed with continued precautions. Encouraging movement, massaging, and dismissing the symptom all risk worsening an injury and losing important information.

Slow bleeding from an organ such as the spleen can continue for hours before compensation fails and shock becomes apparent. Delayed allergy, reduced blood production, and pain alone do not account for the volume loss that produces shock.

Combativeness in a trauma patient often reflects hypoxia, hypoglycemia, or brain injury rather than a genuine refusal, and those causes are treatable. Assuming intoxication, restraining reflexively, and accepting a refusal without documentation all fail a patient who may lack capacity.

Cutting around adherent material avoids tearing away skin that is still attached to it, while removing the rest of the clothing stops ongoing burning. Pulling it free strips viable tissue, prolonged soaking causes heat loss, and leaving all clothing may allow continued injury.

Blocking cerebrospinal fluid drainage can raise intracranial pressure and increase the risk of infection, so the fluid is allowed to flow into a loose dressing. Packing, firm pressure, and nose blowing all obstruct or force flow in the wrong direction.

A patient who is compensating can deteriorate rapidly, and only repeated assessment detects the change in time to act. Billing, anxiety reduction, and arbitrary documentation counts are not the clinical reason for repeated assessment.

Significant mechanisms can produce injuries that remain silent during the compensated period, so evaluation is based on more than the current exam. Releasing the patient, repeating an exam that will be equally normal, and waiting for symptoms all risk missing a developing injury.

A sling and swathe supports the weight of the arm and limits shoulder movement, which is what stabilizes a clavicle injury. Traction splints are for femur fractures, splinting straight increases discomfort, and raising the arm worsens the injury.

A torn diaphragm allows abdominal organs to herniate into the chest, compressing the lung and impairing ventilation. The injured diaphragm loses rather than gains function, the lungs are not necessarily punctured, and the diaphragm does not produce fluid.

A pressure dressing controls bleeding while allowing circulation to continue beyond the wound, which is confirmed by checking the distal pulse. Eliminating the pulse makes it a tourniquet, loose application does not control bleeding, and its use does not depend on tourniquet removal.

Alcohol blunts pain perception and alters mentation, which hides injuries and makes assessment unreliable. Attributing findings to intoxication, assuming low injury risk, and expecting better symptom reporting all lead to missed injuries.

Spinal immobilization takes priority, and the fractured leg is secured during packaging, often to the uninjured leg and the board. Applying traction first delays spinal protection, ignoring both injuries allows further damage, and asking the patient to stabilize his own leg is unreliable.

Compression of the oculomotor nerve by rising intracranial pressure produces a dilated pupil on the affected side, which is an ominous finding. Direct eye trauma can also cause it, a small minority have naturally unequal pupils, and alcohol does not produce unilateral dilation.

Shock is treated based on the physiological findings, and a hidden internal source is assumed until proven otherwise. Waiting to identify the source, attributing findings to anxiety, and limiting care to oxygen all delay treatment of a life-threatening condition.

The restraint stops the body while internal organs continue forward, which can tear vessels and attachments even when external injury is minimal. Belts reduce total energy transferred to the occupant, restraint injuries are not limited to the chest wall, and restrained occupants fare far better overall.

Jewelry that becomes trapped by swelling acts as a tourniquet, so it is removed early while it still slides off. Leaving it in place, deferring removal to the hospital, and applying tight bandaging all risk compromising circulation.

Moist sterile covering with a protective shield prevents drying and further injury while the eye is left in position. Replacing it, applying pressure, and forcing the lid closed all risk permanent damage to the globe.

A weakening faster pulse indicates deteriorating perfusion, which prompts a repeat of the primary assessment to find the cause. Continuing unchanged, slowing transport, and deferring the report all delay recognition of a patient who is decompensating.

Immobilizing the bones on either side prevents movement at the injured joint. Splinting the joint alone allows the adjacent bones to move it, immobilizing the whole limb is unnecessary, and permitting movement defeats the purpose of the splint.

Longer transports increase the opportunity for deterioration, so planned reassessment intervals and preparation for changes are essential. Reducing monitoring, assuming stability, and delaying departure for paperwork all increase risk to the patient.

The skin covers the entire body and forms the primary barrier against pathogens, which is why any break in it creates an infection risk. The liver, lungs, and stomach all serve essential functions but none acts as the body's outer protective barrier.

A fracture is any break in a bone, whether complete or partial. A sprain involves stretched or torn ligaments, a strain involves muscle or tendon, and a dislocation is displacement of bones at a joint.
Ligaments connect bone to bone, and injury to them is called a sprain. A strain involves muscle or tendon, a fracture is a broken bone, and a contusion is a bruise of soft tissue.
A contusion is a bruise, where vessels bleed into tissue beneath skin that remains intact. An abrasion scrapes the surface, a laceration cuts through it, and an avulsion tears a flap of tissue away.
An abrasion removes the outer skin layers through friction against a surface. An avulsion tears a flap loose, a puncture is a narrow deep wound, and an amputation is complete removal of a body part.

Mechanism of injury describes how the energy was applied to the body, which predicts what may be injured. The injuries themselves, the treatment plan, and elapsed time are all separate elements of the assessment.

Bruising around the eyes without a direct blow suggests blood tracking from a basilar skull fracture. A brief headache, a tender scalp bump, and transient dizziness are all common after minor head impacts.
Tissue continues to be damaged until the source of heat or chemical is removed, so stopping the process limits the injury. Area estimation, cause determination, and dressing application all follow.

Hemorrhage, whether internal or external, is by far the most common cause of shock after injury. Allergic reactions, infection, and psychological responses cause shock or shock-like presentations far less often in trauma.

Penetrating trauma involves an object breaching the skin and entering the body, as with stab and gunshot wounds. Force without skin breakage is blunt trauma, temperature exposure causes thermal injury, and repeated stress causes overuse injury.

Each side of the chest can hold liters of blood, so a hemothorax produces major volume loss that is entirely concealed. Electrical activity is not universally affected, blood is not rapidly reabsorbed, and the heart does not fill with air.

Because the skull cannot expand, any increase in volume raises pressure and compresses the tissue and its blood supply. Brain tissue does not swell uniquely, it is richly perfused, and the central problem is the fixed container rather than the resolution rate.

The skin's barrier function is destroyed, so heat and fluid escape freely from the burned surface. Burned tissue does not draw heat from the core, metabolic rate typically rises after major burns, and extensive cooling is avoided precisely because of this risk.

A pedestrian is typically struck by the bumper, thrown onto the hood, and then onto the ground, producing three distinct sets of injuries. Injuries are not confined to the legs or to the initial contact point, and ground impact frequently causes head and spinal injury.

Cold-induced vasoconstriction delays refill even in a well-perfused patient, producing a false indication of shock. Cold does not speed refill, it clearly affects the measurement, and nail beds can still be blanched.

Blood in the pleural space produces dull percussion along with signs of volume loss, unlike air, which produces hyperresonance. Distended neck veins suggest tension physiology, positional sharp pain is nonspecific, and subcutaneous air suggests an air leak.

Burns in this region are readily contaminated by urine and stool, which makes infection a major concern and is why they are referred to burn centers. Nerve endings are present, the burns do not extend into the abdomen, and the area is well perfused.

A child's pliable ribs and bones bend rather than break, transmitting energy to the organs beneath while leaving little external sign. Children's skin is thinner, their organs are proportionally larger and less protected, and force is not dispersed away from the body.

A bleeding patient is likely to need anesthesia and surgery, both of which are complicated by stomach contents, and shock itself raises the aspiration risk. Oral fluids do not meaningfully dilute blood, increase bleeding, or drop blood pressure directly.

Hypoxia and hypotension are the two insults that most worsen outcomes after brain injury, because the injured brain cannot maintain its own perfusion. Low pressure does not protect the brain, the conditions interact directly, and hypotension does not indicate a minor injury.

Hypotension with a narrow pulse pressure and confusion indicates that compensatory mechanisms can no longer maintain perfusion. Compensated shock preserves pressure and mentation, irreversible shock is defined retrospectively, and this is well beyond a normal stress response.

Distended neck veins, muffled tones, and hypotension with clear lungs indicate blood in the pericardial sac restricting cardiac filling. Both tension pneumothorax and massive hemothorax would alter breath sounds on the affected side, and a rib fracture does not cause hypotension with distended veins.

Release of prolonged compression floods the circulation with potassium and metabolic byproducts, which can cause lethal dysrhythmias within minutes. Splinting is secondary, prophylactic tourniquets are not standard practice, and deterioration rather than improvement is the expected pattern.

Internal bleeding requires surgical control, and fifteen minutes to a trauma center is a short interval to spend on transport rather than on scene. Completing an assessment on scene, choosing a facility without surgery, and waiting for a helicopter all add delay without benefit.

Hypertension with bradycardia and an irregular respiratory pattern indicates dangerously high pressure within the skull and impending herniation. This is not adequate compensation, is not explained by a primary cardiac problem, and is not a pain response.

Ischemia time determines the hospital's management decisions, so the application time is documented and communicated clearly. Periodic loosening, removal, and repositioning all risk renewed catastrophic bleeding from an injury that required a tourniquet.

Tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction with a maintained blood pressure are the hallmarks of compensated shock. Hypotension with confusion indicates compensation has failed, and warm dry skin with a normal rate indicates no significant volume loss.

Facial burns carry airway implications and circumferential full thickness burns threaten circulation, so both require specialized care. A small superficial burn and a sunburn can be managed without a burn center.

A flail segment impairs ventilation and usually accompanies underlying lung injury, and absent sounds with tracheal deviation indicate a tension pneumothorax. Isolated rib tenderness and a superficial abrasion are painful but not immediately life threatening.
A significant fall and a shallow water dive both apply axial loading forces to the spine. A kitchen cut and a twisted ankle involve no mechanism capable of producing spinal injury.

Moist coverage prevents drying, and flexing the knees reduces tension on the abdominal wall. Replacing organs introduces contamination and injury, and a dry pressure dressing damages the exposed tissue.

Wounds are exposed and covered before the splint conceals them, a neurovascular baseline is established before the device is applied, the splint is secured without compromising flow, and the reassessment confirms circulation remains intact.

The chest is exposed so every wound is found, breath sounds and effort establish the baseline, an occlusive dressing stops air from entering the pleural space, and ongoing monitoring detects a tension pneumothorax if one develops.

Early loss produces no measurable change, compensation then raises the heart rate while preserving pressure, decompensation follows with falling pressure and declining mentation, and irreversible organ injury develops last.

Hazard assessment with early resource requests comes first, the vehicle is stabilized so it cannot shift onto patient or rescuers, life threats are addressed as access allows, and removal follows once the scene is secured.

A gentle attempt with lubrication may succeed, and the hospital has ring cutters when it does not. Cutting the finger is obviously inappropriate, leaving it without any attempt allows swelling to worsen the constriction, and prolonged icing delays care without resolving the problem.

With a possible skull fracture, packing can force material toward the fracture and blocking drainage can raise intracranial pressure. Tilting the head back causes blood to be swallowed, and ice does not address the concern with this mechanism.

A trauma patient who becomes quiet and withdrawn after being agitated is often deteriorating rather than settling, as cerebral perfusion falls. Interpreting the change as calm, resolved pain, or evidence against injury misses a patient who is declining.

Embedded objects are left in place for removal under controlled conditions, since removal can cause bleeding or leave fragments. Field removal, pushing the object deeper, and applying a tourniquet for a minor wound all cause unnecessary harm.

Triage directs limited resources toward the patients most likely to survive with prompt intervention. Complete treatment one at a time, proximity-based selection, and responding to the loudest voices all misallocate limited resources.

A fall from height with back pain suggests a vertebral fracture, and neurological symptoms can appear later if the spine moves. Attributing the pain to a strain, to positioning, or to the surface he was lying on all risk allowing that movement to occur.

Limiting movement and supporting the limb during every transfer is what reduces pain and prevents further injury. Moving quickly increases the movement at the fracture, self-movement is unreliable, and waiting for pain to subside leaves the fracture unstable.

Firm manual pressure, followed by a tourniquet for extremity wounds, escalates the control appropriately. Repeated inspection disrupts clot formation, elevation alone does not control arterial bleeding, and cold does not stop significant hemorrhage.

Brief factual updates support the family without interrupting care or overstating what is known. Prognostic predictions exceed the provider's scope, refusing to speak is needlessly harsh, and false reassurance can be devastating if the patient deteriorates.

Shock threatens life immediately, so perfusion is addressed while the open wound is covered, with definitive splinting during packaging or transport. Prioritizing the splint, treating only the visible injury, and deferring all care leave the perfusion deficit untreated.

Cooling stops the burning process, and cutting around the adherent material avoids stripping away skin that remains attached to it. Peeling and scrubbing both remove viable tissue, and leaving the garment entirely intact may allow continued heat transfer.

Perfusion findings combined with a mechanism capable of producing injury are what raise suspicion for concealed bleeding. A general complaint, a remote history, and hospital preference provide no evidence of ongoing internal blood loss.

Prolonged entrapment in cold conditions combines hypothermia, which impairs clotting, with the metabolic consequences of prolonged compression. Focusing only on trauma, assuming cold is protective, and using consciousness to exclude hypothermia all miss significant complications.

Worsening distress after sealing a chest wound suggests air is accumulating under pressure, and briefly lifting the dressing allows it to escape. Reinforcing the seal traps more air, permanently removing it allows air to enter again, and additional oxygen does not relieve the pressure.

Padding to support the limb in the position found with movement as a unit limits pain and further injury. Traction splints are for midshaft femur fractures, walking risks displacement, and forced straightening causes additional damage.

The brain is highly sensitive to reduced oxygen delivery, so confusion, agitation, or drowsiness often appear before pressure falls. Mental status is not related to coverage, is one of many documented findings, and a change is never dismissed as expected.

An adult auto-injector delivers 0.3 mg of epinephrine intramuscularly. The 0.15 mg junior device is the pediatric strength, and 1.0 mg is the cardiac-arrest IV/IO dose given by ALS — not a dose an EMT gives by auto-injector.

The 0.15 mg junior auto-injector is intended for children roughly 15-30 kg, so a 22 kg child falls squarely in that range. Auto-injectors come in fixed strengths and cannot be partially administered, and withholding epinephrine in anaphylaxis is never the safer choice.

Anaphylaxis that does not improve after an initial dose commonly needs a repeat, typically 5-15 minutes later, and many systems allow a second auto-injector on standing order or after contacting medical direction. Antihistamines are far too slow for airway compromise and shock, and a smaller pediatric dose would make the undertreatment worse.

The device is designed to be pressed firmly against the anterolateral thigh (the vastus lateralis), where the large muscle gives fast, reliable absorption, and it will fire through ordinary clothing — which matters when seconds count. Auto-injectors are not an intravenous route, and the thigh is preferred over the buttock.

Epinephrine acts on alpha receptors to constrict vessels (raising blood pressure and reducing airway edema) and on beta receptors to dilate bronchioles and increase heart rate and contractility — so it works on all three of the things killing the patient at once. It does not block histamine (that is what antihistamines do, far more slowly) and does nothing to the allergen itself.

Field guidance for suspected acute coronary syndrome is 160-325 mg of non-enteric-coated aspirin, chewed rather than swallowed. Chewing exposes far more surface area to the oral mucosa and speeds absorption, which is the whole point when the goal is to inhibit platelet aggregation as quickly as possible.
